</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#evening_sitting">

<heading>EVENING SITTING.</heading>

<p>Business was resumed at 8 p.m.</p>

<speech by="#minister_of_native_affairs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF NATIVE AFFAIRS</person></from>

<p>moved that the Bill be referred to a Select Committee for consideration and report, with power to take evidence and call for papers, the committee to consist of: Mr. Merriman, Sir Bisset Berry, Colonel Harris, Messrs. Stockenstrom, Bosnian, Chaplin, Geldenhuys, Creswell, and the mover.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#du_toit">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">G. J. W. DU TOIT</person> (Middelburg)</from>

<p>seconded.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#keyter">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. KEYTER</person> (Ficksburg)</from>

<p>moved, as an amendment, that the committee consist of ten. He said he wished to add the name of the hon. member for Frankfort (Mr. Brain) because it seemed to him that the Free State was being ignored.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#theron">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. S. THERON</person> (Hoopstad)</from>

<p>seconded.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_native_affairs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF NATIVE AFFAIRS</person></from>

<p>said he had no objection.</p>

<p>The amendment was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#speaker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">SPEAKER</person></from>

<p>said the hon. member (Mr. Keyter) would have to give notice to move that the name of the hon. member for Frankfort be added.</p>

<p>The motion, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#prisons_and_reformatories_bill_in_committee">

<heading>PRISONS AND REFORMATORIES BILL.<br/>IN COMMITTEE.</heading>

<p>On clause 1,</p>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>moved certain amendments in the Dutch copy of the Bill.</p>

<p>The amendments were agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 2,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. Juta</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said the word &#x201C;officer&#x201D; was not defined. Was the hangman an &#x201C;officer&#x201D;? (Laughter.) He moved the omission of the word keeper from line 92, and that the clause stand over.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from><span class="col_1165-1166" refersTo="page_0592"/>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>did not think a definition of the word &#x201C;officer&#x201D; was necessary, as it meant the holder of an office.</p>

<p>It was agreed that the clause should stand over,</p>

<p>Clause 3 was slightly amended in Dutch.</p>

<p>On clause 5, Officers of convict prisons and gaols,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>moved the deletion of sub-section 4 and the substitution of the following: &#x201C;There shall be for every convict prison and for every gaol a medical officer, who shall either be appointed by the Governor-General, and give the whole of his time to the duties of his office, or shall be appointed by the Minister, and give part of his time to the duties of his office. If no person has been so appointed by the Governor-General or the Minister, or if the post of medical officer be vacant at any convict prison or gaol, the district surgeon shall carry out the duties of medical officer&#x201D;; certain amendments in the Dutch version, which do not occur in the English version, and in line 47, after &#x201C;appointment made,&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;by the Minister.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>thought it was a pity that the Minister had not given notice of the amendments, as it was difficult to follow them. (Cheers.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>said he did not see any provision for the payment of a medical officer. He thought that should be attended to.</p>

<p>The amendment was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 6, Appointment and removal of officers,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>considered that the punishment for making a false statement prior to appointment was excessive oven it were made wilfully. He thought also that the intimation that a man should be liable to dismissal if he married without the consent of the director was unnecessary and harsh. A man would probably be a more efficient officer if he were married. He hoped that the Minister would see his way clear to excise this clause. (Hear, hear.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said he did not agree with the hon. member for George. He thought that it was of the highest importance that a prison officer should make correct statements. Now the matter of age was important because of the pension to which a man would become entitled. On the second point he thought it a very sound principle end&#x2014;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central):</from>

<p>What? (Laughter.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>Very indispensable, and the hon. member for Port Elizabeth should agree with me. Continuing, he said that they had to have unmarried men because it was necessary that many of the prison officials should sleep on the premises. There were other reasons why this provision should not be excluded from the terms of the measure.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>said that the Minister had not appreciated the remarks of the hon. member for George, whose point was that the penalty should only rule in cases where the statement was of a material character. So far as the marriage question was concerned, he pointed out that in a private firm a man would be dismissed for a false statement, whereas in this case the Minister would have a man convicted of perjury.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>pointed out that the English version of clause 4 was totally different to the Dutch version. (Laughter.) It was no laughing matter. In the Dutch version it was stated that a subordinate officer who was unmarried at the time he was taken into the service might be dismissed if he married without permission. According to the English copy it did not matter if the man was unmarried or not, but it depended on whether he was enrolled as unmarried. The only reason adduced by the Minister was that married men were not able to carry out all their duties. Dismissal was the proper way of dealing with these matters. Clause 3 was a marvellous clause, under which, he thought, no court would convict. He considered that the Minister should withdraw both clauses.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>thought that the penalty should be dismissal.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis):</from>

<p>But why should it be neccessary to convict a man in court?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>moved an amendment to the effect that any contravention of the clause should, result in the dismissal of an official and the forfeiture of his pension rights.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#stockenstrom">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. STOCKENSTROM</person> (Heidelberg)</from>

<p>asked whether if the false declaration were made on oath in the Transvaal Province a man would not be punishable in any case?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person>:</from>

<p>That is so.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alexander">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">M. ALEXANDER</person> (Cape Town, Castle)</from>

<p>urged that the clause in regard to false declarations should be withdrawn, as, the Minister had got sufficient protection under existing legislation. As to sub-section 4, he was opposed to that altogether, because he thought the State would be setting a bad example to the general community. (Hear, hear.) It would be a very bad thing for the country if they were to place on the Statute-book a law discouraging marriage. He, therefore, moved that sub-sections 3 and. 4 be deleted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that he was quite prepared to accept the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cape Town, Central. (Hear, hear.) In regard <span class="col_1167-1168" refersTo="page_0593"/>to the remarks of the hon. member for the Harbour Division, he must say that he could not see what the hon. member found different in the Dutch from the English. The English said &#x201C;subordinate enrolled as unmarried,&#x201D; and the Dutch, which he read was, he declared, the same. (Dissent.) He could not possibly accept any amendment which would do away with sub-section 4, because it would be fatal to the public service in respect of its gaols if they were to accept it. &#x2018;They seemed to be very sentimental about getting people to marry and getting a large population in South Africa, but that was just what they had not got to deal with in this case. They were now considering the requirements of the public service.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>submitted that there was no necessity for the clause, because a man could always be dismissed if he could not do his work. He again pointed out that the Dutch was not the same as the English in this clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>submitted that there was a great deal in what had been said about the State discouraging marriage. That, he pointed out, was a subject of great complaint against the banks. The clause was very blunt as it stood, and it might at any rate be toned down a good deal.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>thought it would be fatal on the part of the House to place the power in the hands of any Government to restrain or restrict a man from getting married if he were in a position to maintain a wife.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watt">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. WATT</person> (Dundee)</from>

<p>referred to the practice which had been adopted in regard to the Natal Province, and said that he should support the motion to strike out the clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fitzpatrick">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. P. FITZPATRICK</person> (Pretoria East)</from>

<p>asked how long would a man be likely to serve before he was allowed to get married? He should be against the clause if it meant putting a bar upon a man marrying for, say, 12 or 15 years.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe)</from>

<p>said he hoped the hon. member would press the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#becker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. C. BECKER</person> (Ladismith)</from>

<p>said that he sympathised with the Minister in this case, because, in his own experience as a visiting Magistrate, he had had more trouble with the three married; men who were employed as convict guards than with all the nine unmarried men who were so employed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>assured hon. members of the difficulty of getting married men to do night work, and if some provision were not made in that regard a great many would have to go, because men were required at night-time, and one could not get them to live with their families near gaols. He would propose an amendment to sub-section 4, because he thought the English was incorrect. (Hear, hear.) His amendment was to delete the words &#x201C;enrolled as unmarried,&#x201D; and to add the words, &#x201C;who was unmarried when enrolled.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#duncan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. DUNCAN</person> (Fordsburg)</from>

<p>said that on the question of marriage be thought there was a good deal to be said on behalf of the arguments advanced by the Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that in reply to the point raised by the hon. member for Pretoria East (Sir Percy Fitzpatrick), he wished to say that, judging from what was taking place in the Transvaal to-day, a man need only be a few years in the service to get married.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alexander">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">M. ALEXANDER</person> (Cape Town, Castle)</from>

<p>said he wished to withdraw his amendment to sub-section 3 in favour of that proposed by the hon. member for Cape Town, Central (Mr. Jagger.) He would, however, press his amendment to sub-section 4.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fitzpatrick">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. P. FITZPATRICK</person> (Pretoria East)</from>

<p>inquired if the law was to apply to the existing force?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>replied in the negative.</p>

<p>The amendment moved by the hon. member for Cape Town, Central (Mr. Jagger) was put, and declared carried.</p>

<p>The amendment moved by the Minister of Justice was also declared carried.</p>

<p>The amendment to sub-section 4, moved by the hon. member for Cape Town, Castle (Mr. Alexander), was put, and declared negatived.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alexander">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">M. ALEXANDER</person> (Cape Town, Castle)</from>

<p>called for a division.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers)</from>

<p>rose to a point of order. He said that a hon. member crossed the floor of the House after the tellers had been appointed. He asked that the Speaker be called in to give a ruling.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chairman">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">CHAIRMAN</person></from>

<p>said the point could be raised later.</p>

<p>The division was then taken, on the question that sub-section 4, proposed to be omitted, stand part of the clause.</p>

</speech>

<p>Walton, Edgar Harris.</p>

<p>Watt, Thomas.</p>

<p>Whitaker, George.</p>

<p>Wilthire, Henry.</p>

<p>C. J. Botha and J. Hewat, tellers.</p>

<p>The amendment therefore dropped.</p>

<p>The clause as amended was agreed to.</p>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers)</from>

<p>asked for a ruling on the point he had raised, as to whether a member could leave his seat after tellers had been appointed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chairman">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">CHAIRMAN</person></from>

<p>said that his ruling was that the member who had left his seat after tellers had been appointed must have his vote recorded on the side which he had left.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers):</from>

<p>Oh, I don&#x2019;t want that.</p>

<p>On clause 8,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smuts">

<from>&#x2020; General <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. SMUTS</person> (Ermelo)</from>

<p>considered the clause too severe, because it stipulated that official residences would have to be vacated within 48 hours if required. It might happen that a widow would be called upon to leave within 48 hours of her husband&#x2019;s death.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>pointed out that 48 hours&#x2019; notice was required. No official with a proper sense of his duty would eject a widow within 48 hours of the husband&#x2019;s death.</p>

<p>The clause was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 9,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#hewat">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HEWAT</person> (Woodstock)</from>

<p>said he thought proper provision should be made for hospitals for the chronic-sick prisoners. On Robben Island they had convicts who had been guilty of criminal acts running with boys and other innocent sick people. They ought, he considered, to have special hospitals for criminals, instead of allowing them to associate with the innocent sick in places like the Old Somerset Hospital and Robben Island.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>fully agreed with the hon. member, but lit all depended on the funds provided by Parliament.</p>

<p>The clause was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 11, keeping journal in convict prison by superintendent,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said he thought the same ground was covered more fully in clause 20 (duty of gaoler to keep a journal). He moved that the clause stand over.</p>

<p>It was agreed that the clause should stand over.</p>

<p>On clause 13, establishment of local gaols and road camps,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from><span class="col_1171-1172" refersTo="page_0595"/>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>proposed an amendment, the object of which was to enable a gaol to serve one or more districts, to add at the end of the clause the following new sub-section, viz.: &#x201C;(3) For the purposes of any law relating to courts of resident magistrate a gaol established to serve one or more districts, or a road camp, shall be deemed to be the gaol of the district wherein that court is sitting.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said the sub-section raised a very good principle, and one which he believed the House would endorse, and that was: that no first offenders convicted of petty offences should pass through a gaol. It should be the aim of the Minister to prevent this, but he noticed that the words &#x201C;as far as practicable&#x201D; were used. That meant that several would pass through gaol. To obviate this, he would move that the words &#x201C;as far as practicable&#x201D;, be deleted in line 56.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#berry">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. BERRY</person> (Queen&#x2019;s Town)</from>

<p>said it seemed to him that the cardinal principle in the Bill was to prevent people getting into gaol. People in other countries were giving a great deal of attention to this question, and had established short detention schools. This would, he thought, meet a want which the road camps did not meet. In line 54 he moved to insert the words &#x201C;detention schools or.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>supported both amendments. He believed the Bill was an excellent one, but there was one thing that the Minister had forgotten, and that was: that he had not the money to: put his good intentions into practice. The Bill would upon the Statute-book, but for years it would remain inoperative. This was a measure for which the Minister should demand the money, because if they did not pay in this way now, they would have to pay very much more later on. (Hear, hear.) It was quite delightful to see how many people were now taking such a lively interest in this prison reform. Everyone knew that when a child first went to gaol, it was with a feeling of horror, but after being there once or twice, gaol ceased to terrify, and the descent became easy. Anything almost was preferable to sending children to gaol, where they would associate with criminals of the lowest type.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>moved a new sub-section 3, having formal reference to the &#x201C;gaol of the district.&#x201D; Dealing with the amendment of the hon. member for Cape Town, Harbour (Sir H. Jute), he said that if it were carried into effect 90 per cent of the first offenders would simply receive nothing but the sentence of the Court. A &#x201C;road camp,&#x201D; he went, on to explain, was a place of confinement near to the working place of the people who were there. It was a Transvaal institution, and was a safeguard against these people being contaminated by the vices of gaol-birds. Moreover these people &#x2014;sent there for petty offences&#x2014;did not bear the stigma of having been in gaol. European waifs and strays would be sent to an industrial home, and juvenile offenders to a reformatory. These boys at Heidelberg were put through a process which be believed was going to make them serviceable members of society. He thought this law provided for the class of people whom the hon. member for Queen&#x2019;s Town wished to be provided for. In regard to the point raised by the hon. member for the Harbour Division, as to the treatment of juvenile first offenders who had been convicted of a petty offence. General Hertzog drew the hon. member&#x2019;s attention to section 50 (sub-section 2).</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said that it was no use referring him to section 50, which was never going to be carried out. He appreciated the difficulty that the [Minister had in many places in this country, where an offender was punished, to get him at once into a road camp. He would, therefore, withdraw his amendment, to delete &#x201C;as far as practicable,&#x201D; but in order to ensure that the passing through a gaol should be temporary and not permanent, he moved to insert after &#x201C;goal&#x201D; the words &#x201C;except for the purpose of transit from the place of punishment to the road camp.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#berry">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. BERRY</person> (Queen&#x2019;s Town)</from>

<p>urged the Minister to take power to establish short detention schools.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>said that the clause was one of considerable importance, and he would suggest that the Minister might allow it to stand over.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>said that the hon. member for Queen&#x2019;s Town should move his amendment when the House came to consider the question of reformatories. He promised that he would meet the hon. member if sufficient provision were not already made.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#berry">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. BERRY</person> (Queen&#x2019;s Town)</from>

<p>withdrew his amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>appealed to the hon. member for Cape Town, Harbour (Sir Henry Juta) to withdraw his amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said he hoped the Minister would accept, his amendment, because he had had experience as a Minister of Justice, and he knew perfectly well that unless the House insisted upon it, first offenders would remain in gaol. As they were now legislating on good lines, he thought they should do something to make the Act a practical Act, and not merely a paper Act.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>said they must stick to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cape Town, Harbour (Sir Henry Juta). The intentions of the Minister were good, but what he lacked was the means of carrying out his good intentions. One sum of &#x00A3;50,000, spent in <span class="col_1173-1174" refersTo="page_0596"/>a few parts of the country in providing detention houses, was worth all they put on the Statute-book. They must have places where these people could be sent to. He hoped the amendment would be pressed to a division, if necessary.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said it was impossible to have road camps everywhere for people convicted of petty offences. What could they do at place&#x2019;s like Stellenbosch and Paarl? Juvenile offenders were provided for later on in the Bill. He did not think the proposal to establish road camps was practicable. Some other way would have to be found.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>thought they should make it imperative under the Bill to establish road camps in districts containing a certain number of inhabitants, instead of leaving it permissive.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>said that if the Minister would give him a couple of hundred thousand pounds, he would give him something practical within a fortnight. It was a question of money.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watkins">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. H. WATKINS</person> (Darkly)</from>

<p>referred to the difficulty of dealing with juvenile offenders. They could not be sent to gaol or to a road camp, but they might be sent to a detention school, which might be a private house. He hoped that the amendment of the hon. member for Queen&#x2019;s Town would be adopted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>did not think detention schools were included in the scope of that Bill.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_justice">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF JUSTICE</person></from>

<p>moved to report progress.</p>

<p>The motion was agreed to, and leave obtained to sit again to-morrow.</p>

</speech>

<adjournment>

<p>The House adjourned at <recordedTime time="1911-02-13T23:30:00">11.30 p.m.</recordedTime></p>

</adjournment>

<speech by="#walton">
