<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>supported the amendment of the hon. member for Hope Town. Though he considered it his duty to assist the Government, he was no less obliged to watch the interests of his constituents. The Government had altogether eight million acres of Crown lands in the North-western districts, which produced a tremendous number of locusts <span class="col_1499-1500" refersTo="page_0759"/>How, then, could they expect farmers to destroy those locusts at their own, expense, but for the benefit of the whole country? He much regretted the fact that the amendment had been greeted with derision, because it was an eminently fair one.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#joubert">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. J. J. JOUBERT</person> (Lydenburg)</from>

<p>said he could not support the hon. member for Hope Town. If it were true that some farmers in the North-western districts of the Cape lived too for to be able to report the presence of locusts, one had to suppose that they also lived too for the police to come and worry them.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#cronje">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. R. CRONJE</person> (Winburg)</from>

<p>said that representatives of Free State constituencies could hardly vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Hope Town, because they themselves had a Locust Destruction. Act in the Free State. Co-operation was essential, because no individual could do any good by his own unaided efforts in a matter of that nature.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#mentz">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. MENTZ</person> (Zoutpansberg)</from>

<p>said it had been proved that stringent locust regulations were quite practicable in his constituency, which was by no means a small one. Why should Prieska complain if Zout-pansberg acquiesced? Why postpone the matter? Surely, it would not take a year to let constituents know that henceforth they were to report the presence of locusts to the polioe!</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#vosloo">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. VOSLOO</person> (Somerset)</from>

<p>said it was all very well for the Government to order farmers about, but what of the Government themselves? They owned, altogether, about twenty millions of acres of Crown lands in the Cape, and he thought Ministers had introduced ill-considered legislation. If they provided the farmers with sprays and poison, locusts would soon be destroyed. He would not vote against the clause, however.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#clayton">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. F. CLAYTON</person> (Zululand)</from>

<p>urged that there could not be any serious objection to the clause under debate. No duty was laid upon anybody until they reached clause 18. Surely clauses 16 and 17 could be allowed to pass.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>hoped that the amendment would be withdrawn, as the subject had amply been discussed at the second reading. His constituents and the people of the Transvaal wanted that legislation, and he thought that they could not delay it. The question was: Were not locusts a plague, and if so, should they not do their best to exterminate them? He thought that they should do all they could to exterminate locusts. (Cheers.) If that amendment were passed, the delay would only mean shelving the whole matter. In the Transvaal they had been very successful in combating the locust pest, and he only desired that they should follow up that success. (Hear, hear.) No case for delay had been made out. If constituents were consulted, every clause would be objected to for some reason or other, and the amendment was quite unacceptable. People who owned thirty thousand acres of ground could not be looked upon as poor, and should certainly be able to contribute something towards ridding the country of a pest, that retarded its progress. The destruction of locusts was a comparatively early matter if they were up and doing. If the Government indeed possessed eight millions of acres in Prieska, the hon. member for that constituency could set his mind at rest, because in that case his constituents could not be held responsible for a very large tract. The Government would look after its own ground, and had successfully carried out locust destruction there in the past. Private owners should emulate that example.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>said that the hon. member for Prieska had hurled an accusation at that side of the House, which he thought ought not to go unchallenged. He had said that because when an amendment was moved from the Ministerial side of the House, it was received with laughter from the Opposition side. It would be manifestly unjust if such a thing were allowed to go unchallenged. (Hear, hear.) He could assure the hon. member that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hope Town had been very carefully considered. It was absurd to say that they must go back to their constituents on every possible question. The Transvaal had done well in reward to the eradication of locusts. All that the Prime Minister now asked for v/as the same power as they had had in the Transvaal.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>said that in that instance he could not agree with his hon. friends who represented the North-west. He did not think it would help them to postpone that matter. The Prime Minister, however, did not seem to realise the peculiar conditions existing in the North-west, and he hoped that some consideration would be shown to the people there. He hoped that the hon. member would withdraw his amendment. The matter would have to be tackled in any case but the Bill required amending if it was to become a practical measure.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#aucamp">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. AUCAMP</person> (Hope Town)</from>

<p>said that he was not going to withdraw his motion, even if he were the only one who voted for it. Hon. members could easily speak of the Transvaal, where they had almost exterminated locusts, but the same state of affairs did not exist in his district, and to try to kill off the locusts was like trying to empty a river bucket, by bucket. They must get at the source, and unless they could do that it was no use trying to combat the evil, because there was an in exhaustible supply of locusts. His constituents were against that Bill, and his duty was to vote against these provisions. If he did vote for it, he need never go back to his constituents. (Laughter.) The Bill was impracticable, and would lead to useless expenditure, i.e. <span class="col_1501-1502" refersTo="page_0760"/>taxation. There was no immediate danger of a locust invasion, and it was only fair to consult the country.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#van_niekerk">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. A. VAN NIEKERK</person> (Boshof)</from>

<p>said he could not support the previous speaker. The Government were going to assist the farmer in fighting locusts, whereas the Free State law did not even grant the farmer that measure of relief, so that the Bill, as for as he was concerned, was an improvement on the old order of things.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#vermaas">

<from>&#x2020; Commandant <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. C. W. VERMAAS</person> (Lichtenburg)</from>

<p>applauded the Bill. He had suffered much from locusts, and trusted the Government would pursue a vigorous policy in fighting them.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#serfontein">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. J. SERFONTEIN</person> (Kroonstad)</from>

<p>opposed the amendment of the hon. member for Hope Town, because delay would only lead to reiteration of the objections against the clause next year.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#neethling">

<from>&#x2020; Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. M. NEETHLING</person> (Beaufort West)</from>

<p>said he could not understand the attitude of the hon, member for Hope Town, if an owner were ignorant of the presence of locusts, how could he be expected to notify the police?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wessels">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. H. W. WESSELS</person> (Bechuanaland)</from>

<p>said the Prime Minister&#x2019;s speech showed that the right hon. gentleman was not quite au fait. The Crown lands he, the speaker, had referred to, were situated on the Western border, and the Government did absolutely nothing on these lands with regard to locusts. Farmers in that region had large tracts of country, which they used for stock-breeding only. The locusts, therefore, did not trouble them, in the least, in fact they were rather glad to see them because the insects kept the grass fairly short and did away with the necessity of burning the veld. Why should people in those circumstances be burdened with the destruction, which was solely for the benefit of people living farther east?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>said the previous speaker had not shown a proper spirit. The Government were not desirous of acting to the detriment of a large part of the Union. The Cape had annually spent large sums on locust destruction, but unsuccessfully. If the new Government introduced fresh measures, it was not to impoverish the people, but to save them from being ruined Sprays and poison would be supplied gratis. Experience bad shown that locusts were not batched in Bechuanaland only. The insects hatched there would migrate and lay their eggs elsewhere, so that the next generation was hatched out in another part of the country. Hon. members made too much of the difficulties involved in getting at the locust. In the Transvaal there had been general co-operation, and large swarms had been destroyed. He again opposed delay. He could not understand farmers allowing their veld to foe eaten off by the locust, because such a course was harmful to the country.</p>

<p>Mr. Aucaamp&#x2019;s motion was negatived.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>moved to add after &#x201C;in writing,&#x201D; the words, &#x201C;or otherwise.&#x201D; He said he moved &#x201C;or otherwise&#x201D; so as to deal with the natives. He did not want them to have the excuse that they could not write.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>supported the hon. member for Potchefstroom, but moved, as a further amendment, that notice should be given as soon as the owner could possibly do so.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wessels">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. H. W. WESSELS</person> (Bechuanaland)</from>

<p>supported the previous speaker. The law would be carried out by magistrates, who were apt to punish a main for not giving notice immediately, even though such a course might not have been possible to the farmer.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#kuhn">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>also supported the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#becker">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. C. BECKER</person> (Ladismith)</from>

<p>said that it the amendment were adopted they might as well say good-bye to the prospect of locusts being reported.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#van_niekerk">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. A. VAN NIEKERK</person> (Boshof)</from>

<p>said the clause again referred to regulations. Those regulations were not property explained to the farmers, who might thus contravene them without knowing what they were doing. He moved that no farmer should be punished for the contravention of regulations with which he was unacquainted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#mentz">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. MENTZ</person> (Zoutpansberg)</from>

<p>supported the previous speaker. In this particular case, he thought regulations would be superfluous.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>hoped that the first amendment would not be passed, as it would simply mean a loophole for evasion Be agreed that there was too much legislation by regulation.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#kuhn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>moved after &#x201C;knowledge&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;with reasonable speed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>said some of the people in isolated pants of the country could not always immediately leave their homes to make a report, especially seeing that sometimes that would mean a day&#x2019;s journey.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>said he could not see his way to accept the amendment moved by the hon. member for Clanwilliam. He would suggest the addition of the words &#x201C;without undue delay,&#x201D; in the provision about notice. The regulations were meant to provide for questions being put to the owner as to the size of swarms, nature of the soil, etc., which information was required by the department. He opposed the suggestion of the hon. member for Boshof.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>appealed to the Minister to accept his amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#cronje">

<from><span class="col_1503-1504" refersTo="page_0761"/>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. R. CRONJE</person> (Winburg)</from>

<p>said he could not support the Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#meyler">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. M. MEYLER</person> (Weenen)</from>

<p>asked what was the use of having Bills drafted if they were to be watered down in that fashion? Let them stick to the Bill and take up a strong policy.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>withdrew his amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#kuhn">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>moved an amendment on the lines indicated by the Minister of Education.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#van_niekerk">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. A. VAN NIEKERK</person> (Boshof)</from>

<p>said that if the amendment was adopted, questions might arise as to what was, and what was not, &#x201C;undue delay.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>said he did not think there would be any difficulty about that, because there was no great hurry. The eggs would not be batched until after the first rains.</p>

<p>The amendments proposed by the Minister of Education, Mr. Neser, and Mr. Kuhn were agreed to.</p>

<p>The amendment proposed by Mr. Van Niekerk was negatived.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nicholson">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">R. G. NICHOLSON</person> (Waterberg)</from>

<p>moved: In line 11, after &#x201C;location,&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;or the occupier (if he be a native) of land which is not in a native location or reserve&#x201D;; in the same line, before &#x201C;kraal,&#x201D; to omit &#x201C;the&#x201D; and substitute &#x201C;each&#x201D;; in line 12, after &#x201C;given,&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;by him &#x201D;; and in the same line, after &#x201C;headman,&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;or chief, as the case may be.&#x201D; &#x2020; The MINISTER OF EDUCATION read the section as it would appear if the amendment were adopted, and put it to the committee whether it would not really amount to a contradiction. He pointed out the difficulty of finding a headman where the land was under the joint occupation of several natives.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nicholson">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">R. G. NICHOLSON</person></from>

<p>pressed his amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>pointed out that the owner was obliged to report. &#x201C;Owner&#x201D; included occupier.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_lands">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF LANDS</person></from>

<p>supported the Prime Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nicholson">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">R. G. NICHOLSON</person> (Waterberg)</from>

<p>said he was not convinced that his amendment should he dropped.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>asked what would have to be done in cases where there was no chief or headman, if the amendment were adopted? The clause would meet all circumstances likely to arise.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wessels">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. H. W. WESSELS</person> (Bechuanaland)</from>

<p>said that sub-section 3 was not clear, and that the amendment of the hon. member for Waterberg (Mr. Nicholson) was necessary. The scope of the clause should be widened.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smuts">

<from>&#x2020; General <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. SMUTS</person> (Ermelo)</from>

<p>pointed out that there was some difference between the Dutch and English versions of that clause of the Bill, because, he thought,</p>

<p>&#x201C; bezitter&#x201D; was not exactly the same as &#x201C;occupier.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>said that if the hon. member looked at the definition of &#x201C;bezitter&#x201D; in the Bill, he would see there was no difficulty involved.</p>

<p>The amendment moved by Mr. Nicholson was negatived.</p>

<p>Clause 16 was then agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 17,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>moved that the words, &#x201C;a copy&#x201D; should be omitted, and &#x201C;the import&#x201D; substituted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis):</from>

<p>Is there any penalty for not transmitting?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person>:</from>

<p>Yes.</p>

<p>Agreed to.</p>

<p>Clause 17, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 18,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>moved to add at the end of the clause:</p>

<p>&#x201C; In consultation with and on the advice of the department, by which material for such destruction shall be provided free of charge.&#x201D; He said this was the practice at present in force in all the Provinces. By it they would do a great deal indeed to fight the disease. Without a little sympathetic consideration of this kind he was afraid the law would remain a dead letter.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>moved in line 16 to insert the words &#x201C;by such means at his command&#x201D;; to delete the word &#x201C;immediately&#x201D; in the same lime, and at the end of the clause, to insert &#x201C;and aid the department in carrying out all the provisions of section 17, the materials for such destruction to be provided by the department-free of charge.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chairman">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">CHAIRMAN</person>:</from>

<p>That involves expenditure. I can&#x2019;t put it.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam):</from>

<p>Then I will take out &#x201C;free of charge.&#x201D; At the end of the clause he moved to add &#x201C;and shall aid the department in carrying out the provisions of the Act.&#x201D; Wihiat, asked the hon. member, could one man do against a host of voetgangers? He could not be held responsible, and the object of his amendment was to charge the Government with the destruction&#x2014;only, the farmer should assist.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>said he could not possibly accept the amendment&#x2014;(cheers)&#x2014;which he thought was wrong in principle. He thought the onus should rest more immediately on the man who was going to be benefited&#x2014;the owner of the property. Another reason why he could not accept the amendment was that it was contrary to the Constitution. He had obtained the consent of the Governor-Genenal to pay for the material, but he had <span class="col_1505-1506" refersTo="page_0762"/>not authority at the present time to go beyond that.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#aucamp">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. AUCAMP</person> (Hope Town)</from>

<p>modified his amendment to the effect that the occupier should do everything in his power to assist the official appointed by the Government in connection with the destruction of such voetgangers.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#kuhn">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>said the difficulties in connection with the carrying out of the Bill centred in the clause under discussion. It was altogether impracticable, and, if the committee passed the clause, they might as well tear up the Bill, which would become a dead letter. The clause went much too far. How could they expect people to go 20 or evert 30 hours on horseback in order to obtain material for the destruction of voetgangers? Por the matter of that, by what right could the Government compel farmers to destroy voetgangers, at the latter&#x2019;s expense, at all? His objections to clause 16 were but trifling, compared to the difficulty he felt in connection with the present clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#neser">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. NESER</person> (Potchefstroom)</from>

<p>said the opposition to the present chapter passed his understanding. He quoted from the Bill to show that it was the department which, in the first instance, would look after the destruction of locusts. Killing a swarm really involved very little trouble, and there was no reason why the farmer should be relieved from all responsibility.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#cronje">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. R. CRONJE</person> (Winburg)</from>

<p>said that the (Minister&#x2019;s amendment had removed any objection he might otherwise have felt in connection with the clause. It was not right for the hon. member for Prieska to paint matters in the darkest possible colours, and to imply that all the Government wanted was to ruin the farmer.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>quoted from his experience to show the impracticability of holding farmers responsible for the destruction of voet-gangers.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#venter">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. VENTER</person> (Wodehouse)</from>

<p>moved an amendment to the amendment of the Minister of Education, in order to ensure for the farmer Government assistance in destroying the locusts.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>said hon. members were going just a little too far. All the opposition to that part of the measure seemed to originate in the North western districts of the Cape He did not know why that should be so, but the Northwest appeared to be a peculiar sort of country, where people could not even tackle a locust. He was going to have a look at that country before long. (Hear, hear.) Evidently, farmers up there expected the Government not only to pay for all the material, but to send a commando to fight the insects. The owner of the farm, it appeared, was to sit tight and do nothing. The Bill bad been drafted so as to smooth over all difficulties as for as possible, but the Government could not consent to placing on the Statute-book a law through which they might drive a wagon with sixteen oxen! It was his duty to protect the people, and that duty he was going to carry out in the Bill.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smuts">

<from>&#x2020; General <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. SMUTS</person> (Ermelo)</from>

<p>said they might as well tear up their laws as frame them in such a manner that anyone could escape through the meshes. He opposed the amendment of the hon. member for Hope Town. If anything had been required to convince him that the measure was urgently required, these speeches made on the subject would have done so. It would not do to condemn the Bill just because the need for it might not be felt in one particular part of the country.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#grobler">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. W. GROBLER</person> (Rustenburg)</from>

<p>supported the clause as printed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wessels">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. H. W. WESSELS</person> (Bechuanaland)</from>

<p>moved to report progress.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>opposed the motion. He thought the matter had been sufficiently threshed out, and they should come to a decision without further delay.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#kuhn">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>said he thought the Government showed unreasonable haste. He supported the motion.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>considered the motion unfair. The hon. member for Prieska had had every opportunity of ventilating his opinions, but did not bring forward any new points of view. There was so much important work ahead that it was bad policy to spend an unreasonable amount cm time over one measure.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>said that the amendment had not been fully debated by any means. He supported the motion.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>said his hon. friends were most unreasonable. He respected the opinions of the hon. member for Prieska (Mr. Kuhn), but in this matter the hon. member did not represent the opinions of a large number of farmers in his constituency. Hon. members had been nearly eight hours discussing three clauses, and they could see from the tone of both sides of the House that if they talked about the matter for a fortnight they would not alter it. Hon. members had expressed their opinions dozens and dozens of times and the House was against them. Surely, if they wished to register their opinions they could call for a division, but don&#x2019;t let them ask to report progress and then go on for another day with the same result. (Hear, hear.)</p>

<p>The motion to report progress was negatived.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#aucamp">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. AUCAMP</person> (Hope Town)</from>

<p>said that the clause did not provide for locusts trekking from, say, his neighbour&#x2019;s farm <span class="col_1507-1508" refersTo="page_0763"/>on to his own. He moved an amendment to cover that contingency.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>opposed the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#kuhn">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>repeated his objections to the clause. How could an owner be compelled to &#x201C;immediately exterminate&#x201D; locusts when they appeared on his farm? The Government should alter this to read that the owner should do everything in his power. He much regretted; the fact that the Government compelled hon. members to turn night into day in order to force the Rill through.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#prime_minister">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">PRIME MINISTER</person></from>

<p>said that, if only the eggs were destroyed in time, the trekking of locusts would be out of the question. If immediate notice were given of the appearance of the insects, the Government would be able to check their movements, and to establish reliable data on which to conduct a campaign. A stringent law of a similar character had been carried out in the Transvaal for the past three years, and in no single instance had it been found necessary to punish anyone. The majority were eager to see the law introduced, and they could not allow that majority to suffer for the sake of pacifying a small minority.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alberts">

<from>&#x2020; Commandant <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. J. ALBERTS</person> (Standerton)</from>

<p>said he could not support the amendments moved by hon. members from the North-western districts of the Cape. It was impossible to saddle Government with the entire responsibility of locust destruction.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wessels">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. H. W. WESSELS</person> (Bechuanaland)</from>

<p>said that majorities and minorities had been referred to. He could not see the justice, however, of placing iniquitous burdens on the shoulders of the minority for the benefit of any majority. The swarms in his constituency were much larger than elsewhere. It was improper to force the Bill through against the wishes of the Government&#x2019;s own supporters. That was not the way to treat hon. members on that side of the House.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#de_jager">

<from>&#x2020; Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. L. DE JAGER</person> (Paarl)</from>

<p>thought hon. members representing the North-west were atrabilious. Where the country was too dry to allow of poison being mixed, the Government would surely stay its hand. Hon. members would not meet with insurmountable difficulties in facing their constituents if the matter were properly explained to the latter. They should at least make the attempt, rather than obstruct the passage of the Bill.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam),</from>

<p>in replying to the last speaker, said his constituents were doing their very best; they could not very well be asked to do more! It was all very well for Parliament to make laws, but who would carry them out? He trusted the Government would not resort to extreme measures in forcing the Bill through committee.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#de_waal">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. DE WAAL</person>, (Wolmaransstad)</from>

<p>considered the amendment of the hon. member for Hope Town superfluous.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#aucamp">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. AUCAMP</person> (Hope Town)</from>

<p>said he saw that his best plan would be to desist from, moving any further amendments. As for as he was concerned, he had done his duty, and he could afford to wash his hands of the Bill.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#kuhn">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>said that he would continue to raise his voice against he clause under discussion.</p>

<p>Mr. Aucamp&#x2019;s amendment was put at 11.52 p.m., and negatived.</p>

<p>Mr. Malan&#x2019;s proviso was agreed to.</p>

<p>Clause 18, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 19,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#van_niekerk">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. A. VAN NIEKERK</person> (Boshof)</from>

<p>said that farmers would not understand the word <i>&#x201C;</i> cogluikend&#x201D; (conniving).</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>said the word expressed what was meant.</p>

<p>On clause 20, expenses of locust destruction,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>moved to omit &#x201C;eggs deposited or&#x201D; in line 27.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#kuhn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. G. KUHN</person> (Prieska)</from>

<p>moved to omit &#x201C;or eighteen&#x201D; in line 26. He considered that owners should be held responsible for the carrying out of clause 16 only, and not for that of clause 18.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#midnight">

<heading>MIDNIGHT</heading>

<speech by="#watermeyer">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. B. WATERMEYER</person> (Clanwilliam)</from>

<p>moved to insert &#x201C;wilfully&#x201D; in line 26, section 20, and in line 27 to substitute words to the effect that he shall be liable to pay such amount towards the expenses incurred by the department in destroying voetgangers, as may be assessed by any competent Court, in his presence, judgment for which amount may be executed, in all respects, as a judgment of a Court of Resident Magistrate in a civil action is executed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>hoped that the first part of the amendment would not be pressed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#madeley">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. MADELEY</person> (Springs)</from>

<p>moved an amendment to protect any native from liability who should prove that he had individually endeavoured to comply with sections 16 and 18.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person>,</from>

<p>however, did not think this was necessary.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nicholson">

<from><span class="col_1509-1510" refersTo="page_0764"/>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">R. G. NICHOLSON</person> (Waterberg)</from>

<p>moved to add the following new subsection: &#x201C;(4) In case of land which is not a native reserve or location, but which is occupied by natives only, all such expenses may be recovered pro rata from such male inhabitants of such land as by law are liable to pay native poll or hut tax, in the same manner as any native poll or hut tax is recoverable from these inhabitants.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person>:</from>

<p>I accept the amendment.</p>

<p>The amendments moved by Mr. Kuhn and Mr. Watermeyer were negatived.</p>

<p>Mr. Nicholson&#x2019;s amendment was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wessels">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. H. W. WESSELS</person> (Bechuanaland)</from>

<p>moved an amendment to the effect that Government should be liable for the death of cattle resulting from locust poison. He considered that, whenever the Government took upon itself the responsibility of invading private farms for the purpose of destroying locusts, it should be liable for the consequences of its actions.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chairman">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">CHAIRMAN</person></from>

<p>said he could not accept the amendment, because it would entail extra burdens on the Exchequer.</p>

<p>The amendment moved by the Minister of Education was agreed to.</p>

<p>The amendment moved by Mr. Madeley was withdrawn.</p>

<p>On clause 21,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>moved to omit sub-section (c). It could, he said, be better dealt with under clause 23.</p>

<p>Agreed to.</p>

<p>In clause 22,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>moved after &#x201C;prohibit&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;or restrict. &#x201D;</p>

<p>Agreed to.</p>

<p>The clause as amended was agreed to.</p>

<p>New clause 21:</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wessels">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. H. W. WESSELS</person> (Bechuanaland)</from>

<p>moved a new clause 21, providing that Chapter II. should apply to Crown lands as well las to farms.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chairman">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">CHAIRMAN</person></from>

<p>said he could not accept the amendment, because it involved additional expenditure.</p>

<p>In clause 28,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>moved in line 44 to insert &#x201C;plants&#x201D; after &#x201C;keeping off.&#x201D;</p>

<p>Agreed to.</p>

<p>Clause 8 was reverted to.</p>

<p>The amendment was agreed to.</p>

<p>The Bill was reported with amendments, and the consideration of these set down for Monday next.</p>

</speech>

<adjournment>

<p>The House adjourned at <recordedTime time="1911-03-01T00:23:00">12.23 a.m.</recordedTime> (being Thursday, 2nd March).</p>

</adjournment>

</debateSection>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#opening">

<heading>THURSDAY, March 2.</heading>

<prayers>

<narrative>

Mr. SPEAKER took the chair and read prayers at <recordedTime time="1911-03-02T14:00:00">2 p.m.</recordedTime>

</narrative>

</prayers>

<debateSection name="#petitions">

<heading>PETITIONS</heading>

<speech by="#wessels">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. H. W. WESSELS</person> (Bechuanaland),</from>

<p>from residents at Pokwani, Vryburg, for remission of unpaid instalments due to the Government on the purchase amounts of their farms.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#berry">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. BERRY</person> (Queenstown),</from>

<p>from Sarah C. de Wet, widow of D. J. de Wet, who suffered losses through the late war and never received any compensation therefor.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort),</from>

<p>from G. A. Martin, who was retired from the public service (Cape).</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#neethling">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. M. NEETHLING</person> (Beaufort West),</from>

<p>from C. H. Grove, teacher.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West),</from>

<p>from J. M. Corderoy, retired, from Control and Audit Office, Cape Town.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#reports_laid_on_table">

<heading>REPORTS LAID ON TABLE</heading>

<speech by="#minister_of_public_works">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS</person>:</from>

<p>Public offices at Cradock.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_the_interior">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR</person>:</from>

<p>Draft regulations, census to be taken in 1911.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>brought up the</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#miners&#x2019;_phthisis_compensation_bill_first_reading">

<heading>MINERS&#x2019; PHTHISIS COMPENSATION BILL.<br/>FIRST READING</heading>

<p>The Bill was read a first time, and the second reading set down for Wednesday.</p>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#immigration_restriction_bill_first_reading">

<heading>IMMIGRATION RESTRICTION BILL.<br/>FIRST READING</heading>

<p>The Bill was read a first time.</p>

<p>On the motion that the Bill be read a second time on Monday next,</p>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>said a great deal of interest was being taken in these Bills throughout the country, and he thought members really ought to have more time allowed in which to make themselves familiar with them. He thought the second reading should be postponed to Monday week.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jameson">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">L. S. JAMESON</person> (Albany)</from>

<p>said they knew the session would be coming to a conclusion because of an important event that was taking place elsewhere. Bills were being shovelled into the House at the rate of half-a-dozen at a time. They would like to know what Bills it was proposed to take that session, and which the House would have an opportunity of considering during the recess.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_the_interior">

<from><span class="col_1511-1512" refersTo="page_0765"/>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR</person></from>

<p>said he had no objection to the second reading being deferred for a few days longer. This was one of the Bills which they regarded as essential to pass this session. As to the others, they would have to take their chance in the running.</p>

<p>The Bill was set down for second reading next Monday, the 13th inst.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#public_health_acts_amendment_bill_first_reading">

<heading>PUBLIC HEALTH ACTS AMENDMENT BILL.<br/>FIRST READING</heading>

<p>The Bill was read a first time, and set down for second reading on Thursday next.</p>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#crown_lands_disposal_(execution_of_deeds)_bill_in_committee">

<heading>CROWN LANDS DISPOSAL (EXECUTION OF DEEDS) BILL.<br/>IN COMMITTEE</heading>

<speech by="#vosloo">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. VOSLOO</person> (Somerset)</from>

<p>asked to what extent the Bill affected existing legislation.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_lands">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF LANDS</person></from>

<p>said that no existing law was either amended or abrogated.</p>

<p>The clauses were severally agreed to, whereupon the Bill was reported without amendment.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#third_reading">

<heading>THIRD READING</heading>

<p>The Bill was read a third time.</p>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#zand_rivier_township">

<heading>ZAND RIVIER TOWNSHIP</heading>

<speech by="#minister_of_lands">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF LANDS</person></from>

<p>moved the adoption of the report of the Select Committee on the establishment of the Zand River township, Orange Free State. The Select Committee recommended that, subject to certain conditions and reservations, the application be approved.</p>

<p>The motion was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#explosives_bill_in_committee">

<heading>EXPLOSIVES BILL.<br/>IN COMMITTEE</heading>

<p>On clause 2, interpretation of terms,</p>

<speech by="#baxter">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. D. BAXTER</person> (Cape Town, Gardens)</from>

<p>again raised the question of the position of fireworks under this Bill. Under the definition, he said, explosives would embrace all sorts of fireworks. Under the Gape Act of 1887 dealers in fireworks up to a certain weight were exempted, and if the Minister would accept an amendment to exclude dealers in fireworks not exceeding 100 lb. weight, he thought the position would be met. He moved that after the words &#x201C;explosives magazine,&#x201D; the following be inserted, &#x201C;but shall not include any place for staring or keeping fireworks not exceeding 100 1b. in weight.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that the hon. member laboured under a misapprehension. If he turned to clause 7, sub-section 3, he would find there that a dealer in explosives would have the conditions of his licence marked upon it. That, he thought, got over the hon. member&#x2019;s whole difficulty. The amendment was quite unnecessary, because it was not necessary to store fireworks in separate magazines for explosives.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fawcus">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. FAWCUS</person> (Umlazi)</from>

<p>moved the deletion of &#x201C;fuses&#x201D; from the definition of &#x201C;explosives &#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wilcocks">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. T. M. WILCOCKS</person> (Fauresmith)</from>

<p>hoped that the Minister would not accept the amendment for the deletion of &#x201C;fuses,&#x201D; which were most important in connection with mining. Fuses should be carefully handled and stored. Many serious accidents had resulted from defective fuses.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#baxter">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. D. BAXTER</person> (Cape Town, Gardens)</from>

<p>said that his object in moving the amendment was to make it unnecessary for small dealers to take out a licence under the Act at all. By adopting his amendment, the committee would be following the English precedent.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person>,</from>

<p>replying to the hon. member for Umlazi (Mr. Fawcus), said that in the matter of fuses a dealer would have the conditions of his licence marked upon it, and he saw no difficulty. They must have &#x201C;fuses&#x201D; under the definition of explosives, because they must have power to test them.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#baxter">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. D. BAXTER</person> (Gape Town, Gardens):</from>

<p>Will the small storekeeper have to take out a licence under this Act?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_the_interior">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR</person>:</from>

<p>It&#x2019;s trifling.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#baxter">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. D. BAXTER</person> (Cape Town, Gardens)</from>

<p>said that was exactly what he did not want. The small dealer had to take out a &#x00A3;5 gunpowder licence, and also a &#x00A3;5 magazine licence. He considered that these small people should be treated fairly.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>moved a formal amendment in regard to the definition of chief inspector or inspector of explosives.</p>

<p>The amendment was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chairman">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">CHAIRMAN</person></from>

<p>(to the hon. member for Cape Town, Gardens): Does the hon. member withdraw his amendment?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#baxter">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. D. BAXTER</person> (Cape Town, Gardens):</from>

<p>Yes; there is no use pressing it.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fawcus">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. FAWCUS</person> (Umlazi)</from>

<p>withdrew his amendment, and the clause, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 3, power of Governor-General to appoint inspectors,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>moved that in sub-section 2, the words &#x201C;chief inspector and&#x201D; be deleted, and the deletion of words, for the purpose: of inserting &#x201C;unless the death of any person has been causeed.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#hunter">

<from><span class="col_1513-1514" refersTo="page_0766"/>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. HUNTER</person> (Durban, Central)</from>

<p>said that it seemed to him to be a dangerous principle for an inspector to exercise judicial functions.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that he did not think that any miscarriage of justice was likely to arise. The same principle had worked very well in the Transvaal.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that such a man could not possibly be impartial; but he might have technical knowledge. It might be a Transvaal principle, but to his mind it was a very bad principle.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person>:</from>

<p>If it is a Transvaal principle, that seems to be sufficient condemnation for the hon. member.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central):</from>

<p>I did not say that.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>added that it had worked well in the Transvaal. He assured his hon. friend that there was no reason whatever for an inspector being a party to the business.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (New lands)</from>

<p>said that an inspector was to try a breach of the regulations; but who was to say whether it was a breach or not? There was no appeal anywhere from a decision of an inspector, and he thought that there should be some appeal to the Minister, where a man had been found guilty of a breach of the regulations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that he did not think that the objection was well founded. It was not necessary that the inspector should be the complainant in the case.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea)</from>

<p>also thought that that there should be some appeal from the decision of the inspector.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#silburn">

<from>Major <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. A. SILBURN</person> (Durban, Point)</from>

<p>said that the Bill distinctly said that the inspector might be the judge.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that where the inspector himself was involved in a case, he was not the judge.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#silburn">

<from>Major <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. A. SILBURN</person> (Durban, Point)</from>

<p>said that the clause stated &#x201C;may&#x201D; be, not &#x201C;shall&#x201D; be.</p>

<p>The amendment was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 4, prohibition of manufacture of unauthorised explosives, except in small quantities, for chemical experiment,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>moved that in line 23 the word &#x201C;he&#x201D; be deleted, and the following inserted: &#x201C;such owner or occupier, as the case may be.&#x201D;</p>

<p>This was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 6, prohibition of storage or possession of unauthorised explosives, save in accordance with section 4,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>moved that in line 40 the last two words (&#x201C;of explosives &#x201D;) be deleted</p>

<p>Agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 7,</p>

<p>Verbal amendments were agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 9, no importation or exportation of explosives without permit,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#rademeyer">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. M. RADEMEYER</person> (Humansdorp)</from>

<p></p>

<p>suggested that Magistrates should be allowed to give certificates.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that this was for importation from abroad, and that was very limited nowadays, owing to the enormous manufacture of dynamite in South Africa.</p>

<p>The clause was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 13, particulars to be stated in application,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#baxter">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. D. BAXTER</person> (Cape Town, Gardens)</from>

<p>said the powers of local authorities had to a large extent been taken away in that Bill. Under clause 5 of the Gape Act of 1887, the local authorities had power to say yes or no to the establishment of new explosives factories in their midst. Under the present Bill, all the local authorities could do was to state an objection, but the decision rested with the Commission which considered the application. That raised a rather important point as to whether the night to allow the establishment of explosives factories or stores should not remain in the hands of the local authorities. After all, it was the latter which were responsible for seeing that no damage occurred to the property of citizens. It seemed rather hard to lay down that all that Town Councils could do in this matter was to state an objection.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>did not think it was right that local authorities should have the power to veto in this matter. After all, it was a technical question, and should not be decided by local prejudice, but on the merits of the case. He thought the Bill went quite for enough when it gave the local authorities every opportunity of stating their case to an impartial authority. They might have a suitable locality for a factory, but the local authority might take a very foolish view of the matter, and thus might stop enterprise.</p>

<p>The clause was agreed to.</p>

<p>Clauses 14 and 18 were verbally amended.</p>

<p>On clause 22, licences,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#baxter">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. D. BAXTER</person> (Cape Town, Gardens)</from>

<p>said when it came to the licensing of magazines for the storage of explosives, the definition was extremely wide, and he thought they certainly ought to get the consent of the local authorities before these licences were granted. He would move, therefore, after the word &#x201C;regulations,&#x201D; in line 38, to add the following: &#x201C;and with the consent of the local auhority.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from><span class="col_1515-1516" refersTo="page_0767"/>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>thought unless some words were put in, as the hon. member (Mr. Baxter) suggested, it seemed to him that the inspector would have the power to overrule the local authorities.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#rademeyer">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. M. RADEMEYER</person> (Humansdorp)</from>

<p>thought that Magistrates also should have the power to grant these licences. He moved that the words &#x201C;or Resident Magistrate&#x201D; be inserted after the word &#x201C;inspector.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>pointed out that this was a licence to erect a factory or a magazine. A factory might be very dangerous, and a Magistrate might not know anything about its dangerous nature. It was essential that expert advice should be given before such a licence was granted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>pointed to the fact that there were already licences granted for magazines by Magistrates throughout the country. It would be impossible always to get experts to inspect these places. His hon. friend should differentiate between factories and magazines.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#rademeyer">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. M. RADEMEYER</person> (Humansdorp)</from>

<p>said there were three magazines in Humansdorp, and they went to the Magistrate for these licences. It was not possible to have an inspector stationed there.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea)</from>

<p>said if a man wanted a licence for a magazine, he ought to say what he wanted to keep in it The inspector in his opinion, was the right man to see that it was placed in a safe position. He strongly supported the attitude of the Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe)</from>

<p>said he thought the difficulty could be got over by giving certain discretionary powers to Magistrates to license small magazines.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said there might be a little more time involved, but the taking of the advice of the inspector would insure that the lives of the people would be well protected.</p>

<p>Mr. Rademeyer&#x2019;s amendment was negatived.</p>

<p>Mr. Duncan Baxter&#x2019;s amendment was carried.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea)</from>

<p>moved in sub-section (2), line 41, to omit all the words after &#x201C;on conviction to&#x201D; to the end of the sub-section and to substitute &#x201C;a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds, or, in default of payment, to imprisonment not exceeding three months.&#x201D; He said that he had been in some doubt in regard to moving this amendment. He had discussed the suggested alteration in the clause with the Minister, who apparently was not prepared to agree to it.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#harris">

<from>Colonel <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. HARRIS</person> (Beaconsfield)</from>

<p>also thought the penalty was excessive, considering that the handling of explosives was not so dangerous.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that the hon. member (Mr. Henderson) had argued the matter with him, and, so for from having convinced him, he (General Smuts) thought he had convinced the hon. member.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea)</from>

<p>said there was a hundred times more danger in connection with a factory than there was in connection with a magazine.</p>

<p>The amendment was negatived.</p>

<p>On clause 23,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wilcocks">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. T. M. WILCOCKS</person> (Fauresmith)</from>

<p>said that the clause should lay down the duties of the inspectors.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that the regulations would do so.</p>

<p>Clause 24 was verbally amended.</p>

<p>Oh clause 25, duty of occupier of a factory to make special rules,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>moved a new sub-section (3) as follows: &#x201C;The occupier of any such factory, magazine, or premises shall take all reasonable steps for ensuring or enforcing the observance of any such special rules.&#x201D;</p>

<p>This was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 27, penalties for endangering safety or causing loss of life,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wilcocks">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. T. M. WILCOCKS</person> (Fauresmith)</from>

<p>said the clause did not provide for the employer&#x2019;s responsibility in connection with acts of his employees.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>&#x2020; The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that the responsibility in question existed under the common law.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>moved to increase the maximum penalty for negligently causing an explosion whereby property was endangered from &#x00A3;150 to &#x00A3;250, and for negligently causing an explosion whereby life was endangered from &#x00A3;300 to &#x00A3;500. He also moved that if a person negligently caused an explosion and death resulted, he be made liable to a fine not exceeding one thousand pounds sterling, or in default of payment, to imprisonment with or without hard labour, for a period not exceeding two years.</p>

<p>The amendments were agreed to.</p>

<p>Clause 28 was verbally amended.</p>

<p>On clause 29, power of Governor-General to make regulations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#robinson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. P. ROBINSON</person> (Durban, Umbilo)</from>

<p>said that no sub-section was provided for the qualification of inspectors. It was highly essential that these officials should be fully qualified. A matter of greater importance was that there was no provision either in the Bill or in the regulations to prevent unscrupulous manufacturers from suborning inspectors.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said that the question of suborning inspectors was one for the general law. With regard to <span class="col_1517-1518" refersTo="page_0768"/>the qualification of inspectors, he said that that was a matter for the administration. He moved to add at the end of the clause: &#x201C;The regulations may prescribe daily penalties for a continuing contravention or non-compliance, or increased penalties for a second or subsequent contravention or non-compliance. Different regulations may be made in respect of different Provinces, districts, or areas in the Union.&#x201D;</p>

<p>Agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 30, saving clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watt">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. WATT</person> (Dundee)</from>

<p>referred to the question of small country storekeepers who kept fireworks for sale in retail quantities, and said that as the Bill was framed it would make it impossible for these people to carry on their business. It was a serious matter as for as public convenience was concerned. He moved the following subsection (e): &#x201C;to the beeping for sale of firearms in such small quantities and subject to such conditions as may be proscribed by regulations.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said he was prepared to accept the amendment, which was then put and agreed to.</p>

<p>The clause was further amended and agreed to.</p>

<p>On the schedule,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>moved a number of amendments with regard to certain Acts, the wrong titles of which had been given, and moved that the right titles be substituted.</p>

<p>The amendments were agreed to,</p>

<p>The Bill was reported with amendments, which were set down for consideration on Monday.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#mines_works_machinery_and_certificates_bill_in_committee">

<heading>MINES, WORKS, MACHINERY, AND CERTIFICATES BILL.<br/>IN COMMITTEE</heading>

<p>On clause 10, jurisdiction of inspectors of mines, etc., to try breaches of certain regulations, special rules,</p>

<speech by="#watt">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. WATT</person> (Dundee)</from>

<p>moved in sub-clause 3, line 47, to insert after the word &#x201C;shall&#x201D; the following: &#x201C;With the assistance, if necessary, of an interpreter appointed by the Chief or Resident Magistrate of the district.&#x201D; The object of the amendment was that an interpreter should be present at any trial, if found necessary.</p>

<p>The amendment was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe)</from>

<p>suggested that the words in line 40, &#x201C;or serious bodily injury,&#x201D; might be inserted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>thought that the clause was properly drafted.</p>

<p>The clause reads as fallows: &#x201C;Every inspector of mines, machinery, or explosives may try any breach of a regulation, or of any rule in force under section 5, unless the death of the person has been caused by the breach.&#x201D;</p>

<p>Dealing with, the second sub-section of the clause, which referred to any such officer having the power for a breach of regulations to impose a fine not exceeding &#x00A3;5, and in default of payment the employer having the right to withhold the amount of the fine from the man&#x2019;s wages, and pay it over for the benefit of the Consolidated Revenue Fund,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that the point was that these regulations embraced things for more serious. They were really breaches of the law. Now, be supposed that they wanted to do justice, even to the black fellows. Here they had thousands of men who did not know what the regulations were, and he thought that the case should go for review to the Magistrate. They should not fine a man for something that he knew nothing at all about. He commended that matter to the Minister of Native Affairs, who was the guardian of these people. If he were satisfied that justice had been done, it was not for a private individual to intervene; but it seemed to him that they were doing what might lead to injustice. They did not go for review, but for appeal. What was a barbarian who had never heard of these things to know about lodging an appeal? He wished the Minister of Native Affairs could be induced to pay some slight attention to this matter, which affected people under his guardianship.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>remarked that it would be a very exceptional ease in which natives would be tried for breaches off the regulations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>did not see that at all. White persons could protect themselves, but no distinction was made between whites and natives. Be a man black or white he should have a fair trial, and he was not so certain that a man was going to get justice, except of the Jedburgh variety, in this case.</p>

<p>The clause, as amended, was adopted.</p>

<p>On clause 11, duty of inspectors to inquire into accidents and power to hold inquiries into other matters,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>proposed an amendment making it compulsory to hold an inquiry into accidents of a serious nature.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>maintained that where there was loss of life or serious bodily injury was inflicted an inquiry should be held by a magistrate. We recently had a case in which our own lives were in jeopardy; that was on the railway, and a great hullabaloo was raised that it invariably should be a judicial officer who should hold the inquiry. There was a tendency on the part of the Bill to make the thing a close borough, and to ring the changes between the inspector, the mining engineer, and the officials of the <span class="col_1519-1520" refersTo="page_0769"/>mines. He moved to omit certain words and to insert &#x201C;an inquiry shall be held by a magistrate, justice of the peace, or some officer specially appointed for the purpose.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>moved the insertion after &#x201C;explosives&#x201D; of the words &#x201C;specially appointed by the Minister for the purpose.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>pointed out that in one case a mine, which was on the Limpopo River, was so for away from the nearest town that it would take a week to get there. He did not object to the Minister appointing the person to hold the inquiry, and proposed the insertion of the words, &#x201C;any Government official deputed by the Minister.&#x201D; These inquiries would be into breaches of the regulations. As to the Law Department, that did its work slowly and safely, but in the case of inquiries into breaches of the regulations, no delay would be possible, or mining operations might be held up for a long time.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>did not think an inspector was the best person to conduct an inquiry. (Cheers.) It was very inconvenient, when they were dealing with hundreds of thousands of men congregated in one area for the Minister to pick out an obscure mine hundreds of miles away, and base his argument on that. If a murder was to take place at Leydsdorp, he supposed some judicial inquiry would take place.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person>:</from>

<p>No.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West):</from>

<p>All that I can say is that state of affairs casts more reflection on the territory of my hon. friend than I should have been tempted to cast. He knows that it is not so. Continuing, Mr. Merriman said a ladder down a mine might give way, and five or ten men might be killed. The inspector who had inspected the mine would be responsible for that ladder, and yet he would be put to try the matter. The inspector was not going to blame himself. Some independent inquiry should be held, and he suggested that the clause should be altered so that these inquiries could be conducted by a magistrate, field-comet, justice of the peace, or person appointed by the Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe)</from>

<p>said the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Merriman) had put his finger upon one of the difficulties. The whole of the inspector&#x2019;s time was taken up with fencing regulation after an accident had occurred.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>said he was surprised that the hon. member, with the technical and practical knowledge of the mines he possessed, thought a field-cornet was a man capable of holding an inquiry into a mining accident.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>pointed out that in a certain mining accident, involving serious consequences, the inspector reported that all had been done that could be done, but it was afterwards found that a ladder had not been repaired. A man who was an inspector within a certain area knew the managers of the mines, and he perhaps would not look into an accident with the same keenness as a man who had been specially appointed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said he did not suggest that field-cornets should be called in to inspect highly-complicated systems as the Witwatersrand Mines, but a field-cornet, he thought, was quite capable of inquiring into an accident on a small outlying property.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#sampson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. W. SAMPSON</person> (Commissioner-street)</from>

<p>pointed out that there were only 50 actual inspectors connected with the department. What was really wanted was a better inspection of the mines.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said his amendment was to the effect that an inquiry should be conducted by a magistrate, field-cornet, justice of the peace, or other official appointed for the purpose.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central):</from>

<p>Leave out &#x201C;field-cornet.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West):</from>

<p>Well, I have no objection.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>pointed out that there was an average of 20 inquiries per day in the Witwatersrand alone, which had to be conducted down in the mines. If these had to be conducted by magistrates they would have to increase the bench of magistrates. These inquiries by inspectors only referred to breaches of regulations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said his hon. friend had not read his own Act, because it said nothing about a breach of regulations. It says accidents endangering life and limb, or causing death. What was wanted was some independent man to conduct this inquiry. The statement that there were 20 serious accidents on the Rand was, in his opinion simply a rhetorical flight by his hon. friend.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>pointed out that the Minister did not say that there were 20 accidents; he said there were 20 inquiries, not necessarily breaches of the regulations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_mines">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF MINES</person></from>

<p>objected to his right hon. friend (Mr. Merriman) applying the words &#x201C;rhetorical flight&#x201D; to the statement he made. The inspector inquired into an accident, but he had nothing to do with the result. It might be that someone lost his life, then the matter would be inquired into by the Judiciary. The principle was the same as the Gaika Loop <span class="col_1521-1522" refersTo="page_0770"/>disaster, where an inquiry was held by the railway authorities. If anyone was guilty then the law would take its course, but at the stage where the inspector was called in, it was simply a technical inquiry.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said the matter was a very serious one indeed, because in this sub-section on clause 11, there was no single word concerning any breach of regulations. All that he contended was that a serious accident should be inquired into by a judicial officer or some other independent person. The number of accidents in the Transvaal was sufficiently serious, because he found that in the whole of the mines&#x2014;coal, gold, diamond mines, and so on&#x2014;the rate was about six per diem.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#theron">

<from>&#x2020; Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. S. THERON</person> (Hoopstad)</from>

<p>said that in an accident inquiry a question might arise as to the instructions given by the inspector. If the accident resulted from dereliction of duty on the inspector&#x2019;s part it was not right to put the inquiry into his hands.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that these inquiries were only public in a technical sense. They were not really public inquiries. If a magisterial inquiry were held, it would be open to the press representatives.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#macaulay">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. MACAULAY</person> (Denver)</from>

<p>pointed out that it was a complaint of inspectors that their time was fully occupied with these inquiries, so that they could not devote sufficient time to their duties proper, which were to inspect mines and prevent accidents.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#duncan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. DUNCAN</person> (Fordsburg)</from>

<p>said it did not appear to him how the judicial authorities were to be informed of any accident involving death or endangering life. As for as his experience went, in the majority of these inquiries the public heard nothing about them. He also thought that in accidents causing death or endangering life a full report of the inquiry should be sent to the Attorney-General&#x2019;s Department.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#phillips">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">L. PHILLIPS</person> (Yeoville)</from>

<p>said that pretty well every accident of a serious nature that occurred went into the papers. He did not think there was any accident involving loss of life which did not get into the papers. It certainly could not be said that the public did not know about these cases. In many cases, if they had a judicial inquiry they would not get as good an inquiry owing to the technical matters involved as they would before an inspector.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that the Government inspector was responsible for seeing that the mine was properly conducted. It was a duty cast upon him. He neglected it, through indifference, or, perhaps, owing to casual methods, and a fatal accident took place, say, for instance, the hauling gear was not in order. They then asked that man to carry out an inquiry into the cause of that accident. Was it likely that the inspector was going to say that it was owing to his negligence in inspecting the hauling rope? He would find some other good reason.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#phillips">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">L. PHILLIPS</person> (Yeoville)</from>

<p>said he did not believe that this alteration which it was proposed to effect would make for better inquiries in cases of accident to life and limb than they had under inspectors. It was extremely unlikely in any complicated case of, let us say, a fall of ground, that the Magistrate would elicit any more than the inspectors would.
