<p>thought that the Minister in charge of the Bill should explain sub-section (a). He understood that this meant that the Government did not propose to differentiate between the steamers, but only to differentiate against the goods, that was, against the consignee.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>Yes.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#farrar">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">G. FARRAR</person> (Georgetown):</from>

<p>Well, I think that is perfectly right; and I think that any differentiation against the steamers would have led the Government into a very complicated position.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>The hon. gentleman has stated the position correctly. The differentiation takes place on the quay.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#quinn">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. QUINN</person> (Troyeville)</from>

<p>said that the Government now came to the House with a proposal carrying that mad practice to its worst extreme. What the Government now proposed was this: recognising that the Conference lines&#x2014;if that thing went to its bitter end&#x2014;would do what every other combine would do, and every business man would do&#x2014;fight&#x2014;it said that they were not even going to be allowed to struggle. What the Government now proposed to do was to make it impossible for anyone to use their ships, and then they talked, as an hon. member opposite had done, about the dignity of that position. The Government now came with a pistol to their heads, and said that they would cripple them (the Combine) if they did not agree with what the Government wanted. Most of them were agreed that reforms were necessary, and many of them were agreed that the rebate system was all wrong, but what honest man could agree that that was the right method of fighting the shipping companies? If the House agreed to that, it would be a most reprehensible piece of business.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that he did not see how the Government could have done otherwise than it did, because in the Post Office Bill it was proposed to give the company a very large subsidy, and that naturally was going to keep the combine together. That was really the position. It was now simply proposed to put it outside the power of the Government to make a contract with such a company. He admitted that that was an extreme step; but the case demanded an extreme step; and how otherwise were they going to break the monopoly down? In fact, this was the only method by which they could break it down. In the Straits Settlements some differentiation like that was also made, and that was the only way in which a matter of that kind could be dealt with. Differentiating was exactly what the companies were doing. They had differentiated against Cape Town the other day. (An HON. MEMBER: Why?) To suit their own ends, because they had been called upon to pay their fair share towards the interest and the upkeep of the Docks. A more daring piece of business, showing the monopoly and power they held, had never been shown. It was about time that that power was broken down. Another case of differentiation on the part of the combine was that of a man who shipped outside the ring having to pay 5 per cent. more than one who did not ship outside the ring. The companies took up the right to dictate to this country, and who were to use these docks: who were to land, and who to ship the goods. The question was whether they, as a country, were going to tolerate that sort of thing? To break that monopoly down they had a perfect right to say what they should charge on goods landed in the Docks into which they (the country) had put their money. If they wanted to break down that monopoly, he did not see what other weapon the Minister had.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea)</from>

<p>said that the hon. member for Cape Town was quite wrong, and knew that he was wrong when he said that the Conference Lines were being subsidised by this or any other country. They were simply being paid for any services which they rendered. He did not think the hon. member had put the case fairly.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>interposing: I never used the word &#x201C;subsidy.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea.) (continuing)</from>

<p>said that he would like the Minister in charge of the Bill to give them some information as to how he intended these clauses to be worked if they were passed by the House. What did he mean by saying he would differentiate in dock dues on goods? He (Mr. Henderson) did, not know what &#x201C;dock dues on goods&#x201D; were. How could he differentiate on goods which were landed for transshipment?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>said he hoped his hon. friend would withdraw the amendment he had moved. (Hear, hear.) He believed the existing contract expired in September of next year, and if they were going to do anything of a practical character they had got to do it now, and not six months hence. The hon. member for Durban had said that the company were paid for their services to the country. He (Mr. Henderson) said that they were not paid too much for the services they rendered. But, by the showing of the companies themselves, they had been paid considerably too much for the services they had rendered to the public. The <span class="col_1819-1820" refersTo="page_0919"/>company had reduced their charges. They had recognised, by their own action during the past week, that the rates they had been charging for services rendered to South Africa were excessive. He held in his hand a paper showing the rates that had come into force, or were to come into force, on March 10. This paper showed reductions of a substantial character. The hon. member quoted two or three classes of goods, and instanced mineral waters, on which the rates to Mossel Bay were reduced from 15s. to 12s. 6d., Algea Bay from 15s. to 12s. 6d., East London 17s. 6d. to 15s., and Durban 25s. to 17s. 6d. (Hear, hear.) Surely, his hon. friend, representing such an important mercantile community as Durban, owed a debt of gratitude to the Minister for introducing proposals which had already caused such a substantial reduction in the interests of the port which he represented. They ought to use the lever that they had to their hands for the purpose of obtaining the best terms for the people of this country. The Government ought not to hesitate to exercise the instrument they had in the mail contract for the purpose of assisting the agricultural development of the country. They were not getting as fair rates for the development of their industries as other countries were getting. This was legislation of an extreme character; they had a desperate disease, and it required a desperate remedy. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the result of this Bill would be the emancipation of this country from monopoly of any sort whatsoever.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said he had just listened to one of the violent speeches which reminded him of the old days. His hon. friend would very likely find that he had got this country into a most horrible mess by legislation of this kind. He could not conceive anything more calculated to do what they were told about yesterday, and that was to drive capital out of the country. It was shipping to-day, and it might be dry goods to-morrow. He was prepared when the time came to go fully into this matter, and show that those arguments of the hon. member for Fort Beaufort were simply founded on moonshine. (Laughter.) But he did not think that this was the time to do it. He wanted to see the proposals moved, so that they could argue the matter on its merits or demerits. He would like to ask the Postmaster-General whether there had been any communication with the Imperial Government or the Imperial Post Office with regard to these proposals?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>The Imperial Post Office has been communicated with in connection with matters in so far as the Post Office is affected.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fremantle">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. E. S. FREMANTLE</person> (Uitenhage):</from>

<p>Have they answered?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (to Sir David Graaff):</from>

<p>Have you any objection to laying the correspondence on the table, because this is a very important matter? I want to see exactly where we stand with the Imperial Government, who are the argest partners, and who pay about 60 or 66 per cent.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>said that he agreed with the right von. Gentleman that they need not have half-a-dozen debates on this matter, and that it was superfluous to have a full-dress debate now ana another when they went into committee. The information asked for by his right hon. friend could be placed before them in committee.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said he could not find that the Chamber of Commerce gave him any lead on this object. He thought it would be well if the various Chambers of Commerce representing commerce throughout the country should have an opportunity of considering the proposals. One knew perfectly well that the small trader was totally opposed to the proposals. The big trader, however, wanted to be able to take the matter into his own hands. He thought some time should be allowed so that they could get some guidance from the Chambers of Commerce on this important question.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fremantle">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. E. S. FREMANTLE</person> (Uitenhage)</from>

<p>hoped the hon. member opposite would not press his amendment. He thought they ought to go into committee to consider these matters. He hoped the Minister in charge of the Bill would recognise the extraordinary position in which they were placed, and give the information asked for. He asked for the information which the right hon. member for Victoria West (Mr. Merriman) had asked for. As a matter of fact., he had already asked for the information, but it was not forthcoming. Instead of that the Minister told the House. That he had been writing to the Imperial Government. He (the speaker) dared say he had, but what he wanted to know was what the Imperial Government had been writing to him. (Laughter.) When a grave question was asked the Minister, and he gave anything but a plain answer, he must not be surprised if a great deal of suspicion were created. Another thing he would like to know was whether the Minister was sure of his own proposals, because he introduced proposals which were discussed at great length, then withdrew them, and now introduced a new set of proposals. Were other proposals to be brought forward at a later stage?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#silburn">

<from>Major <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. A. SILBURN</person> (Durban, Point)</from>

<p>said that he, like the hon, member for Cape Town, Harbour (Sir Henry Juta), was anxious to have a lead from the commercial men he represented. The two new clauses were most important and before they were actually considered in this House he thought that it was only right and just that the people he represented should have <span class="col_1821-1822" refersTo="page_0920"/>them before them. He quite understood that the hon. member for Cape Town, Central (Mr. Jagger), was anxious to see the clauses go through, but there were small people who were going to suffer. He thought that in justice to the small people who were going to suffer&#x2014;at present they were able to compete with the big men&#x2014; they should have these clauses put before them, and get their opinions. He was anxious that the people of Durban, especially those connected with shipping, should have an opportunity of discussing them.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#vintcent">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. I. VINTCENT</person> (Riversdale)</from>

<p>said that so far as the Mossel Bay Chamber of Commerce was concerned, it had expressed itself unanimously in favour of the continuance of the rebate system.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central):</from>

<p>Let us have the resolution.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#vintcent">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. I. VINTCENT</person> (Riversdale):</from>

<p>The report appeared in the Cape Town papers one day last week. He read the resolution, and said that although he had no intention of going into the merits of the case, he wished to say that it would be well if consideration of these new clauses were adjourned until the shipping people and others interested had had an opportunity of discussing them.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>withdrew his amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#wilcocks">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. T. M. WILCOCKS</person> (Fauresmith)</from>

<p>then moved a formal amendment, which was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#speaker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">SPEAKER</person>:</from>

<p>I must ask the Hon. the Minister in charge of the Bill whether he proposes to extend the title of the Bill?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_the_interior">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR</person>:</from>

<p>Yes.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>was understood to say that notice had been given.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#hon_members">

<from><person refersTo="hansard_za">HON. MEMBERS</person>:</from>

<p>It is not on the paper.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#speaker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">SPEAKER</person>:</from>

<p>The question is, that the House go into committee to consider the Minister&#x2019;s motion, and, if agreed to, that the House resolve itself into committee, and that the Chairman have leave to bring up a report to-day</p>

<p>The motion to go into committee was agreed to.</p>

<p>On the second part of the motion, that the Chairman have leave to bring up a report to-day,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fremantle">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. E. S. FREMANTLE</person> (Uitenhage)</from>

<p>asked if it were possible to object?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#speaker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">SPEAKER</person>:</from>

<p>Does the hon. member object?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fremantle">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. E. S. FREMANTLE</person> (Uitenhage):</from>

<p>Yes.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#speaker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">SPEAKER</person>:</from>

<p>Well, the motion cannot be put.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#in_committee">

<heading>IN COMMITTEE.</heading>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>moved to omit sub-sections (a) and (b) of the motion.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>asked whether it was wise to take this discussion now? They could not have two discussions on it.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>said that he wanted a full discussion on the matter. If they adopted the motion, and then went into commitee he did not know where they would stand. He withdrew his amendment.</p>

<p>The resolution was adopted, and reported to the House.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#speaker">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">SPEAKER</person></from>

<p>announced that the Chairman would bring up a report tomorrow.</p>

<p>The Bill itself was then considered in committee.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#in_committee">

<heading>IN COMMITTEE.</heading>

<p>On clause 2, interpretation of terms.</p>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved, in the paragraph defining railways, in line 15, after &#x201C;force&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;but shall not include the railway lines of the Department of Railways and Harbours&#x201D;; in line 16, after &#x201C;body,&#x201D; to insert &#x201C;other than the Department of Railways and Harbours&#x201D;; in line 20 to omit &#x201C;thirtieth day of June,&#x201D; and to substitute &#x201C;thirty-first day of March.&#x201D;</p>

<p>The amendments were agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 3, administration and control of the department,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#farrar">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">G. FARRAR</person> (Georgetown)</from>

<p>thought that this was a good opportunity for the Minister to give the House an outline of the policy with regard to the Post Office. During the Minister&#x2019;s second reading speech, they had heard a great deal about the shipping combine, but they had heard nothing as to the Post Office.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said it would be more convenient to answer any question for information as to the administration of the Post Office when the Estimates were under consideration.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>moved an amendment providing that any regulations made should be laid on the table of the House before coming into operation. He pointed out that there was a serious discrepancy between the Dutch and English copies of the Act. In the Dutch edition there were very important omissions as to the conventions and regulations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#chairman">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">CHAIRMAN</person></from>

<p>said that the Minister was about to move an amendment in the Dutch copy.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>moved that the penalties authorised to be imposed by the Postmaster-General <span class="col_1823-1824" refersTo="page_0921"/>far breaches of instructions be limited to &#x00A3;10. He urged that it was not proper to give the Minister or officials unrestricted power to impose penalties.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that this was copied from the old Cape Act, and the law was the same in the Transvaal and Natal, and in Australia.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said he did not think it was a wise procedure to allow the Postmaster-General to inflict penalties without these being specified, as also the offences. He hoped his hon. friend would take the trouble to read the Gape Act.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>What section?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West):</from>

<p>Section 2. I will move an amendment to add the words &#x201C;not exceeding &#x00A3;10 for each offence.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central):</from>

<p>well l, it depends on the offence.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#hunter">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. HUNTER</person> (Durban, Central)</from>

<p>pointed out that these penalties were imposed merely for disciplinary purposes.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said he quite agreed that they should not give the Postmaster-General power to impose penalties without specifying the crimes for which they were to be imposed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said he had no objection to accepting the amendment of the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Merriman), although the amount of &#x00A3;10 was high, and he did not think the Postmaster-General would impose such a penalty.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>said in the railway to-day they had exactly the same power under the old Cape Act, and he proposed to include it in the new Act.</p>

<p>Mr. Merriman&#x2019;s amendment was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Gape Town, Harbour) and Mr. C. L. BOTHA (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>moved amendments in the Dutch version.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_education">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF EDUCATION</person></from>

<p>said that it made no difference in the world. (Laughter.) He thought that the Minister in charge of the Bill could safely take the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#vosloo">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. A. VOSLOO</person> (Somerset)</from>

<p>said that the fault was that the Dutch was too good; most of them did not understand it. (Laughter.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that he did not think that all these amendments were necessary.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#botha">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. L. BOTHA</person> (Bloemfontein)</from>

<p>said that if these amendments were not made, they would be made in another place. That was what had happened already.</p>

<p>The amendment moved by Mr. Struben was negatived.</p>

<p>On clause 4, Postmaster-General to prescribe fees, etc., for services rendered,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved to omit the first four lines, and to substitute the following: &#x201C;The Postmaster-General shall prescribe, and may from time to time alter the fees, rates, or charges to be demanded or received for the conveyance of postal articles and for the transmission, conveyance, or delivery of telegrams, and for any other service rendered by the Department, and may cause to be made and sold postage stamps, envelopes, cards, wrappers, and other articles, embossed or impressed with such amounts of postage as he may deem fit; provided that &#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>said that the Minister of Posts and Telegraphs would admit that clause 4 was not in accordance with Cape lines, because in the Cape Act it had clearly been laid down what charges should be made for services of that kind rendered by the Department; and the House was the proper tribunal to fix these charges. With the exception of sub-section (b) the Postmaster-General had the right at any time to make any charge he liked, without any notice to the House, by putting a notice in the &#x201C;Gazette.&#x201D; He did not think it was proper, and they did not know, when the House rose, which charge the Postmaster-General would make for the registration of letters, parcels post, within the Union, and so forth. He did not think that was satisfactory, and he put it to the Minister whether it would not be infinitely more satisfactory to lay down these charges once and for all in the schedule. He thought that the public ought to know what these charges were, and that they should only be altered by Parliament.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_finance">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF FINANCE</person></from>

<p>said that he did not agree with the hon. member. If the principle were accepted by the committee of fixing the charges in question, the committee would also have to adopt the same principle of laying down a tariff of railway fares and rates. He thought it was customary all over the world to give elastic powers to these executive officers. He thought it would be a hopeless thing to ask the Postmaster General to have to come to the House every time he wanted to alter the tariff of charges of telephones and postal matters. These charges were often regulated by Inter-State Conventions, and it would be impossible, if the proposal of the hon. member were agreed to, to come to any definite resolution unless some elasticity were given like that.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>said that they at the Cape had been at such Conventions since 1882, and had managed to get along some way or other. The case of the Railway Department was not analogous to the Post Office. Surely they ought to know once and for all what the charges <span class="col_1825-1826" refersTo="page_0922"/>for postal matters were; and that they should not be altered at the whim of the Minister.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that he had endeavoured to follow in this Bill Cape lines as far as possible, and wherever there was a difference he had given the public the benefit of it. It was unnecessary to make fixed charges. The rates were fixed by regulation in all countries from time to time, and could not be altered, except with the consent of the Governor-General-in-Council, and then any alteration must be published.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>said it seemed to him that a constitutional point was involved, because the Postmaster-General was given power to impose taxation.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>I think the hon. member is quite wrong. It is not a tax; it is a charge for services rendered. (Hear, hear.) The Postmaster-General does not fix it without the consent of the Governor General-in-Council.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said he would support the clause as it stood.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that, as the clause stood, they might levy preferential rates which might cause gross injustice to certain localities certain individuals, or concerns. It had been suggested that they should trust the Government. He did not trust any Government&#x2014;not a bit further than he could see them (Laughter.) If the clause went through they ought to have some protection that the rate for letters should not be raised to more than one penny. It at present said that the rate should be &#x201C;not less than one penny.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said he did not think they ought to give the Government this power of discretion. It was a bad thing to put in the hands of any Government the power to lower or raise postal rates.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>said he was surprised that his hon. friend the member for Cape Town (Mr. Jagger) had not supported him in his contention that these rates should be laid down once and for all. He hoped the Minister would agree to an alteration of sub-section (a), by giving the public ample notice in the &#x201C;Gazette&#x201D; of any proposed change, say, three months.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>intimated that he could not accept any such alteration, and pointed out that the clause followed the law in the United Kingdom If they fixed anything by schedule, they had to get the schedule repealed before they could alter it. He thought it was perfectly correct that the Governor-General-in Council should have discretion, in this matter.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#phillips">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">L. PHILLIPS</person> (Yeoville)</from>

<p>could not understand why the Minister should propose to fix a minimum and not a maximum rate.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>said he was confident that any change which was made would be in the direction of lowering rather than raising the rates.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>moved to add at the end of the clause a proviso directing that no increase of the fees, rates, or charges should be enforced until six weeks after the first publication in the &#x201C;Gazette.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe)</from>

<p>said it was not clear to him whether the present 1/2d. rates for unclosed circulars were to continue. There was no definition of the word &#x201C;letter&#x201D; in the Bill, and they had no security that this rate would be continued when the Bill became law.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that the object was to provide a differential postal rate for diamonds.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe)</from>

<p>said that his point was that under this clause circulars would in future have to bear a penny stamp.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said the intention was not to raise the rates. The general tendency throughout the world was to lower them.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that the Minister of Posts and Telegraphs stated that he had never known of the rates having been raised in the Cape. Of course not, because that was a matter fixed by schedule.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#farrar">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">G. FARRAR</person> (Georgetown)</from>

<p>complained that although there had been Union for ten months there was no postal guide. He pointed out the differential rates in the different Provinces. For instance, in the Transvaal recently, they made a reduction on newspapers to a non-paying rate. The rate was 1/4d. per newspaper, irrespective of weight. It had not been extended to the Cape Province. If reductions were made, they should see that one section of the community did not get an advantage over another.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said he hoped the Minister would stick to the clause as printed.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour):</from>

<p>Will the Minister kindly give us the meaning of a &#x201C;letter&#x201D;? It has been asked for by the hon. member for Jeppe three times, and he has not yet got an answer.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>Letter is not defined in any Act.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour):</from>

<p>Well, then, what about having a penny stamp?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from><span class="col_1827-1828" refersTo="page_0923"/>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that a letter was a communication which was not open to inspection.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour):</from>

<p>So that what is not open to inspection is a letter?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>Yes.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Gape Town, Harbour):</from>

<p>Well, that is something I never knew. (Laughter.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe):</from>

<p>Will the Minister state in which Act that definition is laid down, because it is not in this Act we are now considering?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>repeated that a letter was not defined in any Act.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>asked the Minister whether he had any intention of arranging that all telegraph offices should be open for one hour on Sundays? It was an absolute necessity.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that he was not prepared to give the hon. member any assurance, but he would look into the question, which was a very big one.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#henderson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. HENDERSON</person> (Durban, Berea)</from>

<p>moved to delete the word &#x201C;penny&#x201D; for the insertion of &#x201C;halfpenny.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>moved the following addition to sub-section (a), &#x201C;such fees, rates, and charges shall, however, not exceed those prescribed by the first schedule to the Cape Colony Act of 1892.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said that he had got the schedule of the Cape Act, and saw that only postcards, newspapers, book packets, and sample packets were carried for a halfpenny. If a circular was not one of these things, and he had never heard that it was, and if it were carried for a halfpenny, then there was something irregular.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that the Department must be given some discretion.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#juta">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. H. JUTA</person> (Cape Town, Harbour)</from>

<p>said that he wished to give the power to the Minister to make the fee less than a penny.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that pressure was always being brought to bear on the Department to take closed letters at 1/2d. for delivery in the same town in which they were posted. That was wrong. The cost of transport was trifling; the real expense to the Post Office was in the collection and delivery, and a letter posted and delivered in Cape Town cost practically the same to the Department as a letter posted in Cape Town and delivered in the Paarl.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>contended it would be a great mistake to place arbitrary powers in the hands of the Post Office Department to increase the tariff, so as to meet a deficiency. In other countries the tariff was fixed. They should fix a maximum rate.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>said the hon. member&#x2019;s (Mr. Nathan&#x2019;s) amendment would fix the same tariff as was provided for in an Act which was to be repealed by this Act. The result would be there would be no tariff at all. (Laughter.)</p>

<p>The amendment moved by Sir D. P. de V. Graaff was agreed to.</p>

<p>Mr. Currey&#x2019;s, Mr. Nathan&#x2019;s and Mr. Henderson&#x2019;s amendments were negatived.</p>

<p>The clause, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 5,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved that clause 5, relating to contracts, the Shipping Combine, etc., stand Over.</p>

<p>Agreed to.</p>

<p>Clauses 8 and 9 were verbally amended.</p>

<p>On clause 15, what is a newspaper and supplement to newspapers,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#duncan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. DUNCAN</person> (Fordsburg)</from>

<p>moved: To add at the end: &#x201C;Notwithstanding anything in this section, all literary publications printed and published in the Union shall, when posted for transmission to any place within the Union be considered to be newspapers within the meaning of this section.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said he could not accept the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#duncan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">P. DUNCAN</person> (Fordsburg)</from>

<p>said the amendment would give a preference to publications printed in the Union.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#sampson">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. W. SAMPSON</person> (Commissioner-street)</from>

<p>supported the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said a monthly publication was carried at newspaper rates.</p>

<p>The amendment was negatived.</p>

<p>Clause 19 was verbally amended.</p>

<p>On clause 22, redirection and interception of postal articles,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved to insert, in line 15, after &#x201C;article&#x201D;: &#x201C;Provided further, that any parcel arrested or intercepted in transit through the post for delivery to the sender or addressee at the office at which such stoppage is effected shall be liable to such fee as may be prescribed in that behalf.&#x201D; The mover explained that the amendment was necessary in order to bring the clause into conformity with the present postal conditions.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>pointed out that the idea of the clause was that a parcel could be stopped at the instance of the sender, but a small fee would be charged.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from><span class="col_1829-1830" refersTo="page_0924"/>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>moved as an amendment to that of the Minister to omit the words &#x201C;other than a parcel.&#x201D; He thought the time had come when in the interests of the public parcels should be considered in the same light as letters or other postal matter.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>How often would it happen that a parcel was addressed Cape Town when it was meant for Johannesburg? I do not think it is worth while burdening the Act with such an amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland):</from>

<p>If there are very few of these cases the Postal Department would not be put to much extra trouble. I merely mentioned the question as a matter of principle.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>said he desired information. When a letter was posted it was no longer the property of the sender, but by this clause apparenly the sender had still control over postal matter. Why should there be any differentiation?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>withdrew his amendment.</p>

<p>Sir David Graaff&#x2019;s motion was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 24, articles which are to be sent by postmasters to Returned Letter Office for disposal,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers)</from>

<p>moved to add at the end of the clause the words &#x201C;or delivered to him if applied for.&#x201D; This amendment, he said, would facilitate business a great deal, and would save the applicant waiting until the Post Office chose to send the letter back.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>accepted the amendment, which was adopted.</p>

<p>Clause 27 was verbally amended.</p>

<p>On clause 28, unclaimed articles elf value and art idles posted in contravention of this Act,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#madeley">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. MADELEY</person> (Springs)</from>

<p>moved to omit the reservation in brackets in the clause, viz.: &#x201C;Unless, any such postal article or the contents thereof have, in his opinion, been posted in contravention of this Act, or with intent to evade payment of the postage properly chargeable thereon.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said the words as they stood in the clause were identical with the present South Africa Act, and they were no innovation.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person> (in reply to Mr. MADELEY)</from>

<p>said that the hon. member would see that it was only done in cases of attempted fraud.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#madeley">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. MADELEY</person> (Springs)</from>

<p>said that if the parcel were confiscated, and the man proceeded against, he would be twice punished. Why Could a man not be given notice, so that he could redeem the article and pay the required charges?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that he had never known of a case when an understamped parcel had been confiscated.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#watkins">

<from>Dr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">A. H. WATKINS</person> (Barkly)</from>

<p>said that a man might have a good reason to give, and he should have the opportunity of being heard. Now he was given no opportunity.</p>

<p>There was some further discussion, in which Mr. MADELEY and Mr. JAGGER joined.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West):</from>

<p>I would like to ask the hon. member for Cape Town, Central, who seems to be in charge of the Bill&#x2014;(laughter)&#x2014;whether he gives the Postmaster-General instructions on the Bill? (Laughter.)</p>

<p>The amendment was negatived, and clause 28 agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 30, delay in transmission, return to sender, or delivery to other than addressee of article prohibited,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>asked the Minister whether he was not conferring upon the sender a power which he should not have?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that a letter should not be interfered with once it had been posted; but in the case of a parcel it was different, because parcels were infinitely more easily traced, and it was possible a parcel might be wrongly addressed. A parcel would not be &#x201C;arrested&#x201D; unless there was a very good reason for it.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>said that he objected to the sender &#x201C;arresting&#x201D; the parcel. He wanted the Minister to provide that this should not take place without the consent of the addressee.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_lands">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF LANDS</person></from>

<p>drew a distinction between letters and parcels. He pointed out that there were certain legal results in one case, but not in the other.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers)</from>

<p>urged that powers should be given to some lower official than the Postmaster-General to arrest parcels, for the protection of traders in other places than Cape Town.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that the provision had worked well in the past.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#alexander">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">M. ALEXANDER</person> (Cape Town, Castle)</from>

<p>said that under clause 3 the Postmaster-General could delegate his powers to the subordinate postmasters.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from><span class="col_1831-1832" refersTo="page_0925"/>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers):</from>

<p>He can, but he won&#x2019;t.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Gape Town, Central)</from>

<p>defended the powers which the Postmaster-General had to arrest letters.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe)</from>

<p>said he could not see any reason for making a distinction between a letter and a parcel.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#schreiner">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. L. SCHREINER</person> (Tembuland)</from>

<p>urged that no distinction should be made.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that there was an essential difference between a letter and a parcel. A letter had no intrinsic value, but with a parcel it was quite different. Mr. Jagger explained the procedure which was adopted for the arrest of a parcel.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#brown">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">D. M. BROWN</person> (Three Rivers)</from>

<p>said he hoped the Minister would make some provision for the power to arrest a parcel to be delegated.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that the present system had worked satisfactorily.</p>

<p>The clause was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 34, articles addressed to persons conducting a lottery or dealing in indecent or obscene matter,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>moved to insert after the word &#x201C;addressed,&#x201D; the words &#x201C;by or.&#x201D; His object was, he said, that the Postmaster-General should be able to detain or delay all postal articles addressed by any person conducting a lottery or dealing in indecent matter to any person in the Union.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_finance">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF FINANCE</person></from>

<p>hoped that the hon. member had considered the effect of his amendment. If it were agreed to, it would place enormous power, in the hands of the Postmaster-General.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said the power was given in clause 30.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that a private letter should be regarded as sacred.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>said that, while anxious to stop lotteries and indecent matter, he thought the amendment, if carried, would give power to the Postmaster-General to destroy the secrecy of private letters.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that he was not prepared to accept the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#struben">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">C. F. W. STRUBEN</person> (Newlands)</from>

<p>withdrew his motion.</p>

<p>On clause 35. notice of departure of vessels,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>moved to insert the words &#x201C;or Postmaster at the port of departure,&#x201D; after the word &#x201C;Postmaster-General,&#x201D; in line 37.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said he was prepared to accept the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>said that the words &#x201C;or agents,&#x201D; in line 1, did not suit the present shipping requirements at all. He was proceeding, when</p>

<p>Business was suspended at 6 p.m.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#evening_sitting">

<heading>EVENING SITTING.</heading>

<p>Business was resumed at 8 p.m.</p>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>thought the words &#x201C;or person in charge of any vessel&#x201D; should be substituted for the words &#x201C;or agent.&#x201D; They would then be following the Cape Act. He was informed that the agent often really had no say in the movements of the vessel; the responsible person was the master, or the person acting as master. The agent was simply the business representative on shore. The word &#x201C;agent&#x201D; could be left out all through the section. The hon. member also pointed out that there was no penalty, as in the English Act, in the case of a person opening a sealed mail bag or taking out a mail bag entrusted to him for conveyance.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that often the agents had charge of the vessels. To leave the agents responsible would give additional security to the Post Office Department. The other matter was covered by clause 96.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>said that clause 96 referred to an officer of the department.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>preferred the term &#x201C;person in charge.&#x201D; There were agents of vessels who had not &#x2018;the power to stop vessels or to give the required notice. There was no difficulty in the case of big vessels at the large ports, but in other instances they would be making agents responsible who were powerless.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that instances had occurred where it was desired to detain vessels for a couple of hours, and the captain could not be found. It would strengthen the hands of the department if they could look to the agent.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said the point was that here they provided for fining an agent &#x00A3;100 when he might be quite powerless to comply with the requirements of the Act.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#madeley">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">W. B. MADELEY</person> (Springs)</from>

<p>suggested the words &#x201C;duly authorised&#x201D; should be inserted before &#x201C;agent.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#searle">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. SEARLE</person> (Port Elizabeth, Southwest)</from>

<p>moved to add to the proviso, &#x201C;and that this law shall not apply to vessels clearing from one port of the Union to another.&#x201D; He pointed out that vessels <span class="col_1833-1834" refersTo="page_0926"/>called at places, like Port Elizabeth, and only stayed a couple of hours. It would be ridiculous to require such vessels to give six hours&#x2019; notice.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that a ship would ordinarily have to get pratique before it could be allowed to leave a port, so that no inconvenience was caused by its having to get the authority of the Postmaster.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>moved to delete &#x201C;six hours&#x201D; for the purpose of inserting &#x201C;three hours,&#x201D; as the period of notice required to be given of the departure of a vessel sailing for a port within the Union.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>accepted this amendment, which was agreed to.</p>

<p>An amendment to substitute &#x201C;eight&#x201D; and &#x201C;six,&#x201D; in place of &#x201C;nine&#x201D; and &#x201C;five,&#x201D; moved by Mr. Jagger, was agreed to.</p>

<p>Mr. Currey&#x2019;s amendment, to insert after &#x201C;Postmaster-General,&#x201D; &#x201C;or the Postmaster at the port of departure,&#x201D; in regard to the authority to allow a shorter notice, was agreed to.</p>

<p>The clause, as amended, was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>moved: That the following be a new clause, to follow clause 35, viz.: &#x201C;36. If a master of a vessel (a) opens a sealed mail bag with which he is entrusted for conveyance; or (b) takes out of a mail bag with which he is entrusted for conveyance any postal packet or other thing, he shall forfeit two hundred pounds.&#x201D;</p>

<p>He afterwards withdrew it.</p>

<p>On clause 36, masters of vessels to convey mails tendered,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved to omit &#x201C;one,&#x201D; and to substitute &#x201C;five,&#x201D; in order to make the penalty for a breach of the section &#x00A3;500.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>thought the penalty for a slight delay of mails was very stupendous. He thought the penalty should fit the crime.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said it would depend on the circumstances of the case.</p>

<p>The Minister&#x2019;s amendment was agreed to.</p>

<p>Clauses 42, 43, 44, 46, 48, 49, and 51 were verbally amended.</p>

<p>On clause 52,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved that the deposits made in one year should not exceed &#x00A3;100, and the total amount of deposits shall not exceed &#x00A3;600.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>thought that the amount of the deposits should not be restricted too much.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>pointed out that a man who was in receipt of &#x00A3;20 or &#x00A3;30 per month, might wish to save &#x00A3;15. They should encourage him to save as much as possible.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>thought &#x00A3;100 a year was quite sufficient, because a man who wanted to save more than that could make different arrangements.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>hoped the Minister would accept the yearly limit of &#x00A3;200, then, when the &#x00A3;600 limit was reached, they could call upon the depositor to make other arrangements.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#orr">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. ORR</person> (Pietermaritzburg, North)</from>

<p>desired to know if they had received any communication from the Associated Bankers on the subject.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said they had made no objection to the amendment that had been moved, and so he believed they were satisfied.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>said if the Minister could not accept the &#x00A3;200 a year they might at least compromise at &#x00A3;150.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_finance">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF FINANCE</person></from>

<p>pointed out that as soon as a depositor had saved &#x00A3;100 he could convert it into a Savings Bank certificate.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fitzpatrick">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. P. FITZPATRICK</person> (Pretoria East)</from>

<p>said the discussion had related so far to men depositors who were able to save &#x00A3;100 a year, but there was the case of women depositors who only save &#x00A3;100 in several years.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>thought it was not desirable that Post Office Savings Banks should compete with ordinary banks. These people were able to have &#x00A3;1,600 in the Savings Bank&#x2014;&#x00A3;1,000 in certificates and &#x00A3;600 on ordinary deposit.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>said he agreed that &#x00A3;1,600 was sufficient limit altogether, but the Minister had originally intended that the limit for one year should be &#x00A3;100. He would like to know if any representation had been made to him upon the matter.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>Yes; very strong representations.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central):</from>

<p>Outside the Government?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person>:</from>

<p>Yes; outside the Government as well.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said these savings banks were simply established to encourage thrift among the poorer classes. When a man saved more than &#x00A3;100 a year he was really doing very well, and could make other arrangements. Banks, he believed, would give 31/2 percent. <span class="col_1835-1836" refersTo="page_0927"/>per annum on a six months deposit. It was not right for the Government to go and interfere with the other banks of the country. He hoped that the Minister would stick to his clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central):</from>

<p>Does this class of man go to a bank? He never sees a bank.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central):</from>

<p>Oh!</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#creswell">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">F. H. P. CRESWELL</person> (Jeppe)</from>

<p>said that he agreed with Sir Edgar Walton. Why place obstacles in the way of thrift?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#nathan">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. NATHAN</person> (Von Brandis)</from>

<p>hoped that the amount which could be invested in the Savings Bank would be unlimited. Why not encourage thrift, and encourage them to put their money in? It was the cheapest way for the Government of obtaining money.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that the limit of &#x00A3;1,000 had been in vogue in the Cape for 20 years, and had worked very well. The Government had &#x00A3;800,000 in Savings Bank certificates; and women also largely went in for this form of investment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that they did not limit a man to investing &#x00A3;100; he was not allowed to invest more than &#x00A3;100 per year in the Savings Bank, but he could invest more if he liked in Savings Bank certificates.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>asked whether it would not be better for his hon. friend when he came to clause 72 to reduce the amount which might be invested in Savings Bank certificates, or do away with them altogether. He wanted to assist the man who did not have any capital, and was trying to lay some by.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fitzpatrick">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. P. FITZPATRICK</person> (Pretoria East)</from>

<p>said that the Savings Bank was the resort of many who tried to put up a fund for the education of their children. If they raised more than &#x00A3;100 they would have to go to another bank, and go through the same procedure, and forfeit the interest if they withdrew any amount. He asked whether the Government could not give depositors a chance of putting in a larger amount than was now allowed, and even cut out the certificates altogether?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_finance">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF FINANCE</person></from>

<p>said that he was perfectly willing to make a compromise, and make an increase in the amount which would be allowed to be deposited in one year, provided a reduction was made in the other clause. He would be perfectly satisfied if his hon. friend (Sir David Graaff) would agree to an amount of &#x00A3;1,000 altogether being allowed to be deposited; &#x00A3;500 and five certificates of &#x00A3;100. (Hear, hear.)</p>

<p>In reply to Sir G. FARRAR (Georgetown),</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_finance">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF FINANCE</person></from>

<p>said that all he had in mind was that nobody should be allowed to have more than &#x00A3;1,000 deposited on the two accounts. The present proposal was to make it &#x00A3;1,600.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said that if that proposition were taken, it was going to discourage thrift.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that these Savings Bank certificates were the most popular form of investment they had, for while the banks gave 3 per cent., they had been giving 31/2 per cent on these certificates.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#orr">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. ORR</person> (Pietermaritzburg, North)</from>

<p>moved that the clause stand down, in order to give the Ministry an opportunity of consulting together, and to place something before the House upon which they could all agree.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>said that he did not think that necessary, because they all accepted the reasonable proposition of the Minister of Finance.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that he would agree to the clause standing over.</p>

<p>It was agreed that the clause should stand over.</p>

<p>Clause 54 was verbally amended.</p>

<p>On clause 55, friendly societies,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>asked for an explanation as to the effect of this clause.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that a provision of this kind had been in existence for many years. Friendly societies, &#x201C;or any other club, society, or fund approved by the Postmaster-General,&#x201D; were allowed to deposit up to the maximum amount without restriction. The societies must be Approved by the Postmaster-General.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>thought that they should lean rather to individuals than societies, and he moved that the words &#x201C;without restriction&#x201D; be deleted for the purpose of making such deposits subject to restrictions specified in preceding clauses.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#orr">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. ORR</person> (Pietermaritzburg, North)</from>

<p>hoped the amendment would not be accepted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_railways_and_harbours">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND HARBOURS</person></from>

<p>pointed out that the provision was made really for the benefit of poor people.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#maydon">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. G. MAYDON</person> (Durban, Greyville)</from>

<p>withdrew his amendment, and the clause was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 56, interest,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved: In line 61, to omit thirtieth day of June in every&#x201D; and to substitute &#x201C;end of every Savings Bank.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir. <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>said that they could not agree to this clause. His hon. friend was taking <span class="col_1837-1838" refersTo="page_0928"/>power to pay interest up to the rate of 5 per cent. If he issued a notice to-morrow that he was going to pay 5 per cent, he would empty all the banks in the country, and, besides, he would be doing something for which the Savings Banks were never intended. He (Sir Edgar) thought the limit should be 31/2 per cent.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#orr">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. ORR</person> (Pietermaritzburg, North)</from>

<p>proposed as an amendment, that the words &#x201C;not exceeding the rate of &#x00A3;5 per cent, per annum&#x201D; be deleted.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#smartt">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. W. SMARTT</person> (Fort Beaufort)</from>

<p>said that if they did not fix some limit us to the rate of interest they might have a Government short of money offering a large rate of interest, which would, as his hon. friend had said, practically clear all the banks of the country. He thought that if they fixed the rate at 31/2 or 4 per cent, it would be a fair amount.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that the present Cape Act of 1883 provided for 5 per cent., although they had never paid more than 31/2 per cent. He thought it was advisable that the Government should have the right to give interest up to 5 per cent. It was possible that the Government might want money, but if the committee were at all strong on the subject he thought that, as a compromise, they might make the limit 4 per cent. Of course, when they said 4 per cent., they did not mean that the Government would pay 4 per cent. He considered that the Government should have the right to go a little higher than the interest actually paid.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central)</from>

<p>said that his hon. friend had given the worst possible reason for this. The Savings Bank did not exist for the purpose of enabling the Government to get money. The Minister must get that idea out of his head altogether. The Savings Bank was for the purpose of giving poor people good security. The inducement was good security, and a fair rate of interest.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#merriman">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. X. MERRIMAN</person> (Victoria West)</from>

<p>said that he must congratulate his hon. friend (Sir Edgar Walton) on having made his first true Opposition speech. (Laughter.) It was the sort of speech that was made by a Treasurer when he got into Opposition. He (Mr. Merriman) always thought that the management of the Savings Bank was an extremely tricky one, but he had never hesitated to use the balances in the Savings Bunk. (Laughter.) He congratulated his hon. friend (Sir Edgar Walton) on his repentance.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#fitzpatrick">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. P. FITZPATRICK</person> (Pretoria East)</from>

<p>said he remembered the time when the rates given by the banks on fixed deposit were 6 or 8 per cent.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said that he quite appreciated what the hon. member for Port Elizabeth (Sir Edgar Walton) had said about not financing through the Post Office Savings Bank. If it were thought that 31/2per cent would meet the case he was prepared to accept lit.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>moved to delete 5 per cent, and to substitute 8 per cent., and after &#x201C;pounds,&#x201D; in line 56, to insert &#x201C;ten shillings. &#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_finance">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF FINANCE</person></from>

<p>said he did not think they should have a higher rate than 31/2 per cent. (Opposition &#x201C;Hear, hear.&#x201D;) He told his hon. friend the Minister that he thought the House would have the good sense to move In 31/2 per cent. (Laughter.)</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said he would accept the amendments.</p>

<p>The amendments were agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 66,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved to omit clause 65, and to substitute the following: &#x201C;66. (1) The Postmaster-General shall keep an account of all sums deposited and paid under the provisions of this Act relating to the Savings Bank, and shall pay in such manner and at such times as the Treasury may direct, to the Public Debt Commissioners for investment by them, the amount of such moneys deposited, provided that the Treasury may authorise the Postmaster General to retain such portions of such moneys as represents a reasonable working balance in connection with the repayment of deposits to depositors. (2) The Public Debt Commissioners shall pay to the Postmaster-General the interest derived from the investment of such moneys, and so much of such interest as is not required for the payment of interest to depositors under section fifty-six of this Act shall be regarded as revenue, and dealt with accordingly.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#walton">

<from>Sir <person refersTo="hansard_za">E. H. WALTON</person> (Port Elizabeth, Central):</from>

<p>What is the object of this new clause?</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>replied that the clause had been redrafted to meet the requirements of the Treasury.</p>

<p>The new clause was agreed to.</p>

</speech>

</debateSection>

<debateSection name="#savings_bank_accounts">

<heading>SAVINGS BANK ACCOUNTS.</heading>

<p>On clause 67,</p>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved to omit clause 67, and to substitute the following: &#x201C;(1) As soon as possible, and in every case within four months after the close of each Savings Bank year, the Postmaster-General shall prepare and render to the Controller and Auditor-General for examination a balance sheet of the Savings Bank and accounts in such form as may be approved by the Treasury of the receipts and payments in connection with the Savings Bank and <span class="col_1839-1840" refersTo="page_0929"/>such other accounts and statements as may be required by the Treasury, and copies of all such accounts and statements shall be sent to the Treasury. (2) The balance sheet, accounts, and statements aforesaid shall be certified and reported upon by the Controller and Auditor-General and submitted to the Minister of Finance and laid before Parliament in the same manner as and simultaneously with the Finance and Appropriation accounts of the Union.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#currey">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">H. L. CURREY</person> (George)</from>

<p>drew attention to the word &#x201C;Treasury&#x201D; in sub-section (1). In the Audit Bill which was being considered &#x201C;up-stairs,&#x201D; the word &#x201C;Treasury&#x201D; there was given a distinct meaning. There was, however, no definition of &#x201C;Treasury&#x201D; in this Bill. They had dropped the use of the word &#x201C;Treasury&#x201D; altogether except in the Audit Bill, and he moved that the word &#x201C;Treasury&#x201D; wherever it appeared be deleted for the substitution of the words &#x201C;(Minister of Finance.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>said he had no objection to the amendment.</p>

<p>The new clause, as amended, agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 68, expenses of working bank to be paid out of money provided by Parliament,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved to delete the following words: &#x201C;and all surpluses or profits arising from the administration of the funds of the bank shall be paid in as revenue of the department.&#x201D;</p>

<p>The motion was agreed to.</p>

<p>On clause 60, amounts standing to credit of any depositor may be paid in to revenue if no deposit or withdrawal made during period of 1-5 years,</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#minister_of_posts_and_telegraphs">

<from>The <person refersTo="hansard_za">MINISTER OF POSTS AND TELEGRAPHS</person></from>

<p>moved in line 45 to omit &#x201C;the Postmaster-General may repay the same to that depositor or person&#x201D; and substitute &#x201C;the Minister of Finance shall, if the Postmaster-General certify that the depositor or person aforesaid is entitled there to, pay such amount out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person> (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>moved that the words &#x201C;sinking fund&#x201D; be inserted in place of &#x201C;revenue of the department.&#x201D;</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#orr">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">T. ORR</person> (Pietermaritzburg, North)</from>

<p>did not think that this was the right place for the amendment.</p>

</speech>

<speech by="#jagger">

<from>Mr. <person refersTo="hansard_za">J. W. JAGGER</person>, (Cape Town, Central)</from>

<p>said he thought they should lay down a policy. They wanted to strengthen rather than weaken the sinking fund.</p>

</speech>
